title: Energy-optimal Scheduling For Clocked Reversible Computing
authors: David Soloveichik Michael C. Thumann
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational dissipation may arise from both information erasure and finite-time operation, although both contributions can in principle be avoided in the absence of space and time constraints. Logically reversible computation can replace erasure with ancilla cleanup, and slow adiabatic protocols can eliminate any excess finite-time dissipation. Under limited memory and in finite time, however, choosing reversible cleanup over erasure requires additional dissipative operations, creating a semi-reversible energy--memory--time tradeoff. We formulate this tradeoff at a fixed operating point of an externally clocked thermally coupled computer, where reversible checkpoint moves and local irreversible erasures have specified effective prices [MATH] and [MATH]. Their ratio [MATH] selects an energy-optimal semi-reversible schedule under a checkpoint-memory bound by trading reversible moves against erasures. For a sequential computation whose dependency graph is a line, we derive an exact separator recurrence and prove that an asymptotically optimal schedule repeats a strictly reversible block followed by one local erasure. Coupling this scheduling theorem to a stochastic-thermodynamic constitutive model shows how temperature, primitive duration, memory, and device-dependent operation costs determine whether the optimal schedule uses reversible cleanup, elective erasures, or erasure at every disposal.
tldr: The paper derives energy-optimal scheduling for externally clocked reversible computers under memory and time constraints, trading reversible checkpoint moves against local erasures.
motivation: Reversible computing can avoid erasure dissipation, but finite memory and finite time force a tradeoff between reversible cleanup and irreversible erasure, requiring a thermodynamic scheduling theory.
method: The authors formulate a semi-reversible energy-memory-time tradeoff at a fixed clocked operating point, assign effective prices to reversible moves and erasures, derive an exact separator recurrence for line dependency graphs, and couple the scheduling theorem to a stochastic-thermodynamic constitutive model.
result: They prove that an asymptotically optimal schedule repeats a strictly reversible block followed by one local erasure, and show how temperature, primitive duration, memory, and device-dependent costs select between reversible cleanup, elective erasure, and erasure at every disposal.
conclusion: The work provides a thermodynamic optimization framework connecting reversible computing schedules to physical constraints on information processing under realistic memory and time limits.

It argues that while both sources of dissipation can be eliminated in principle (via reversible computation and adiabatic protocols), practical constraints of limited memory and finite time force a semi-reversible tradeoff. The authors formalize this tradeoff for an externally clocked thermally coupled computer, introducing effective prices for reversible checkpoint moves (ε_R) and local irreversible erasures (ε_I). The ratio λ = ε_I/ε_R governs the energy-optimal schedule under a checkpoint-memory bound. For a sequential computation with a linear dependency graph, they derive an exact recurrence for the optimal schedule and prove that asymptotically the optimal schedule consists of a strictly reversible block followed by one local erasure. Coupling this scheduling theorem to a stochastic-thermodynamic constitutive model, they show how temperature, primitive duration, memory size, and device-dependent operation costs determine whether the optimal strategy uses reversible cleanup, elective erasures, or erasure at every disposal. The work provides a theoretical framework linking abstract scheduling to physical thermodynamics, with implications for energy-efficient computing.

title: Certifying Nonlocal Spin Quantum Entanglement From Local Tunneling Spectra
authors: Payman Kazemikhah, Ruolun Zhang, Xiangyu Luo, Byunghoon Kim, Yu-Peng Zhu, Md. Shafayat Hossain, M. Zahid Hasan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement is intrinsically nonlocal, whereas tunneling spectroscopy measures one site at a time. We show that this apparent mismatch can be overcome: local tunneling spectra can certify spin entanglement without coherent control or absolute intensity calibration. An exact spin sum rule turns the high-bias conductance into an internal normalization, allowing the inelastic spin-flip weight to place a lower bound on the local quantum Fisher information. Total-spin conservation then fixes the otherwise inaccessible intersite fluctuation, converting two local spectra into a bound on a collective entanglement witness. We incorporate coupling to the substrate through a spectroscopic bound on spin leakage, while a hierarchy of thresholds distinguishes entanglement between the spins from entanglement with their environment. Including instrumental broadening and noise, the resulting certificate holds at a stated confidence level. These results establish a route for extracting nonlocal quantum information from equilibrium local spectroscopy.
tldr: The paper shows that local tunneling spectra can certify nonlocal spin entanglement using spin sum rules and quantum Fisher information without coherent control or absolute intensity calibration.
motivation: Entanglement is intrinsically nonlocal, while tunneling spectroscopy measures one site at a time; this work aims to bridge that gap and certify spin entanglement from local equilibrium measurements.
method: An exact spin sum rule normalizes high-bias conductance, allowing inelastic spin-flip weight to lower-bound local quantum Fisher information; total-spin conservation then fixes intersite fluctuations and converts two local spectra into a collective entanglement witness, including substrate leakage and instrumental broadening/noise.
result: The protocol yields a confidence-level entanglement certificate and a threshold hierarchy that distinguishes entanglement between spins from entanglement with their environment, remaining valid under experimental imperfections.
conclusion: The results establish a route for extracting nonlocal quantum information from local spectroscopy and provide a practical entanglement-certification tool for spin systems.

title: Translation-Invariant Pure States With Exotic Half-Chain Factors
authors: Jinmin Yi Ruizhi Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct translation-invariant pure quasifree fermionic states on the one-dimensional lattice whose half-chain von Neumann algebras are hyperfinite factors of type [MATH] or [MATH] for any [MATH]. Via the Jordan-Wigner-Araki transformation, these yield translation-invariant pure spin-chain states with the same half-chain factors, demonstrating that such factors need not be of type I or III. Each state is the unique ground state of a gapless, translation-invariant parent Hamiltonian with superpolynomially decaying interactions. For any fixed factor type, the interval entanglement entropy can exhibit widely varying growth rates, from arbitrarily slow divergence to nearly power-law growth, showing that entropy scaling does not determine the factor type. In contrast, we prove that gauge-invariant quadratic Hamiltonians with finitely many flavours and exponentially decaying hopping exhibit a dichotomy: their ground states either satisfy an area law with a type I half-chain factor, or have logarithmic entropy growth with a type [MATH] factor. The counterexample was discovered with AI assistance.
tldr: The paper constructs translation-invariant pure fermionic and spin-chain states whose half-chain von Neumann algebras are exotic hyperfinite factors, revealing that entanglement entropy scaling does not determine the factor type.
motivation: It investigates the operator-algebraic structure underlying half-chain entanglement in many-body quantum states, challenging the assumption that entropy scaling alone classifies the relevant von Neumann algebra type.
method: Using quasifree fermionic states, the Jordan-Wigner-Araki transformation, and gapless parent Hamiltonians, the authors construct states with prescribed half-chain factors and analyze their entanglement entropy growth; they also prove a dichotomy for gauge-invariant quadratic Hamiltonians with exponentially decaying hopping.
result: They obtain translation-invariant pure states with half-chain factors of type II or III for arbitrary parameter values, show widely varying entropy growth within a fixed factor type, and prove that quadratic Hamiltonians with finite flavours and exponential hopping either obey an area law with type I factors or exhibit logarithmic entropy growth with type III factors.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that half-chain factor type is not determined by entanglement entropy scaling and provides new operator-algebraic counterexamples in quantum spin and fermionic chains.

In contrast, they prove a dichotomy for gauge-invariant quadratic Hamiltonians with finitely many flavours and exponentially decaying hopping: ground states either satisfy an area law with a type I half-chain factor or have logarithmic entropy growth with a type III1 factor. The counterexample was discovered with AI assistance.

title: Autonomous Thermal Switching Outperforms The Frozen Optimum With Vanishing Correlations
authors: Siyi Deng, Longxing Xu, Zhuolin Ye, Xian He, Jianhui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can autonomous thermal switching outperform the best frozen barrier allocation while keeping system--auxiliary correlations arbitrarily small? We establish this relaxation advantage at fixed lowering budget and visible equilibrium, preserving joint detailed balance. On finite reversible networks, optimal fast switching mixes profiles concentrating the budget on single edges. A three-state model gives a strict gain and its finite-rate threshold. Faster switching preserves the gain while correlations vanish throughout relaxation. Collective and continuous models suggest a colloidal test.
tldr: The paper shows that autonomous thermal switching can outperform the optimal frozen barrier allocation at fixed lowering budget while keeping system-auxiliary correlations arbitrarily small.
motivation: It asks whether relaxation-based autonomous control can provide a thermodynamic advantage over static optimal barrier design without requiring persistent correlations, a question relevant to information thermodynamics and autonomous thermal machines.
method: The authors analyze finite reversible networks under joint detailed balance, derive optimal fast-switching profiles concentrating the budget on single edges, and study a three-state model plus collective and continuous extensions.
result: They find a strict gain over the frozen optimum, identify a finite-rate threshold, and show that faster switching preserves the advantage while correlations vanish during relaxation.
conclusion: Autonomous thermal switching offers a correlation-free relaxation advantage, suggesting a possible colloidal experimental test and broadening the design principles for autonomous thermal control.

The authors frame the problem at fixed lowering budget and fixed visible equilibrium, and they impose joint detailed balance so that the comparison is thermodynamically fair. The central claim is a 'relaxation advantage': optimal fast switching can mix nonequilibrium profiles in a way that concentrates the budget on single edges of a finite reversible network, outperforming any frozen allocation. A minimal three-state model is used to demonstrate a strict gain and to identify a finite-rate threshold below which the advantage disappears. The authors further argue that faster switching preserves the gain while system–auxiliary correlations vanish throughout the relaxation, meaning the advantage is not purchased by residual correlations with the controller. title: Ergotropy Of Nonequilibrium Steady States Beyond The Full Secular Approximation
authors: Xing-Xing Hu, Hui-Yu Yang, Kun Zhang, Xiao-Hui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the generation and activation of ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by cyclic unitary operations, is central to quantum battery research. Positive-temperature thermal states are passive, whereas nonequilibrium environments can sustain nonpassive steady states with nonzero ergotropy. However, the full secular approximation commonly used in Lindblad descriptions can suppress steady-state coherence and obscure its contribution to ergotropy. Using a Bloch-Redfield master equation beyond the full secular approximation, we investigate the ergotropy of the nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) of two exchange-coupled qubits connected to independent thermal reservoirs. The NESS ergotropy of two qubits with the same frequency is entirely coherent and grows quadratically with temperature bias near equilibrium. In contrast, detuned qubits can exhibit incoherent ergotropy. We derive an exact analytical criterion for its activation and show that activation requires the hotter reservoir to be coupled to the qubit with the higher bare frequency. Comparing NESSs obtained with and without full secularization reveals quantitative and qualitative differences in ergotropy that reflect changes in both its coherent and incoherent contributions. The results clarify the mechanisms of NESS ergotropy activation and demonstrate the importance of retaining steady-state coherence beyond the full secular approximation when characterizing stationary work resources.
tldr: This paper studies ergotropy in nonequilibrium steady states of two exchange-coupled qubits using a Bloch-Redfield master equation beyond the full secular approximation, highlighting the role of steady-state coherence in work extraction.
motivation: Ergotropy quantifies the maximum work extractable from quantum batteries, but standard Lindblad treatments with the full secular approximation can suppress steady-state coherence and obscure its contribution.
method: The authors model two exchange-coupled qubits coupled to independent thermal reservoirs via a Bloch-Redfield master equation without the full secular approximation, and derive analytic criteria for coherent and incoherent ergotropy activation.
result: For identical qubits the nonequilibrium steady-state ergotropy is entirely coherent and grows quadratically with temperature bias near equilibrium, while detuned qubits can exhibit incoherent ergotropy whose activation requires the hotter reservoir to couple to the higher-frequency qubit.
conclusion: Retaining steady-state coherence beyond the full secular approximation is important for correctly characterizing stationary work resources, and the results clarify mechanisms of nonequilibrium ergotropy activation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates the ergotropy—the maximum work extractable by cyclic unitary operations—of the nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) of two exchange-coupled qubits, each connected to an independent thermal reservoir. The authors argue that the full secular approximation, commonly employed in Lindblad master equations, can artificially suppress steady-state coherence and thus obscure its contribution to ergotropy. To overcome this, they use a Bloch-Redfield master equation beyond the full secular approximation, which retains coherence terms. They consider two scenarios: identical qubits (same frequency) and detuned qubits. For identical qubits, the NESS ergotropy is entirely coherent and scales quadratically with the temperature bias near equilibrium. For detuned qubits, incoherent ergotropy can emerge. The authors derive an exact analytical criterion for the activation of incoherent ergotropy, showing that it requires the hotter reservoir to be coupled to the qubit with the higher bare frequency. They also compare NESSs obtained with and without full secularization, revealing both quantitative and qualitative differences in ergotropy that reflect changes in coherent and incoherent contributions. The work clarifies the mechanisms of NESS ergotropy activation and highlights the importance of retaining steady-state coherence beyond the full secular approximation for characterizing stationary work resources.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that the full secular approximation can suppress steady-state coherence and thus obscure coherent contributions to ergotropy in quantum batteries.
Shows that for two identical qubits, the NESS ergotropy is entirely coherent and grows quadratically with temperature bias near equilibrium.
Derives an exact analytical criterion for the activation of incoherent ergotropy in detuned qubits, requiring the hotter reservoir to be coupled to the higher-frequency qubit.
Compares NESSs with and without full secularization, revealing quantitative and qualitative differences in ergotropy due to changes in coherent and incoherent contributions.
Provides a detailed analysis of the role of steady-state coherence in work extraction from nonequilibrium steady states.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors model two exchange-coupled qubits, each locally coupled to an independent thermal reservoir, using a Bloch-Redfield master equation that goes beyond the full secular approximation. This approach retains off-diagonal density matrix elements (coherences) that are typically discarded in the secular approximation, allowing for a more accurate description of steady-state coherence. They solve for the nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) and compute the ergotropy, decomposing it into coherent and incoherent contributions. For identical qubits, they analyze the dependence on temperature bias and coupling strength. For detuned qubits, they derive an analytical criterion for the activation of incoherent ergotropy by examining the sign of the incoherent ergotropy. The comparison between full and non-full secular treatments is performed by solving the master equation in both cases and contrasting the resulting NESSs and ergotropies.
deep_read.results_analysis: For identical qubits, the NESS ergotropy is found to be entirely coherent and scales quadratically with the temperature bias near equilibrium, i.e., ℰ ∝ (ΔT)^2. This quadratic scaling is derived analytically and confirmed numerically. For detuned qubits, incoherent ergotropy can become positive, and the authors derive an exact condition for its activation: the hotter reservoir must be coupled to the qubit with the higher bare frequency. This criterion is independent of the coupling strength and detuning, as long as the detuning is nonzero. The comparison between full and non-full secular approximations reveals that the full secular approximation can lead to qualitatively different predictions, such as the absence of coherent ergotropy for identical qubits or incorrect activation conditions for detuned qubits. title: Performance Of A Hot Rb Vapour-Based Portable Quantum Memory

abstract: ArXiv:2610.24098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum repeaters will be paramount to the success of the future quantum internet. Presently however, the losses incurred in fibre communications are unsustainable when fragile quantum states are transmitted over long distances. The most effective repeater nodes will require incorporation of a minimum of two quantum memory units (QMems) for successful operation. Therefore a network composed of numerous nodes will ideally require scalable repeaters that contain QMems that are portable, robust and do not require a high amount of overhead. Here we investigate the performance of a commercial QMem based on a warm vapour of Rb atoms. Specifically, we characterize the coherence time, absolute efficiency, signal to noise ratio and bit error ratio of this device over a range of vapour temperatures that are readily controllable. For our system, we place these performance metrics into the same conventions as those established for current optical communication protocols. Development of QMem systems meeting these benchmarks will be a vital step for seamless integration of QMems systems into present-day communication architectures.

title: Optimal Robust Single-qubit Gates In Superconducting Quantum Processors
authors: Tangyou Huang, Anuj Aggarwal, Jingjun Zhu, Akshay Gaikwad, David Niepce, Marcus Rommel, Andreas Nylander, Amr Osman, Anita Fadavi Rousari, Janka Bizn\'arov\'a, St\'ephane Gu\'erin, Gheorghe Sorin Paraoanu, Anton Frisk Kockum, Giovanna Tancredi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity quantum gates that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections. Here, we develop energy-optimal control pulses for single-qubit gates that are simultaneously robust against frequency detuning and waveform inhomogeneities while also suppressing leakage outside the computational subspace. Combining the optimized pulse envelopes with an adaptive control scheme, we experimentally demonstrate optimal robust gates on a superconducting quantum processor. For a gate duration of 90ns, we achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and 99.6% for Hadamard-type gates. For the X gate, we maintain fidelities above 99.5% for simultaneous drive-amplitude variations up to 20% and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz. This robustness outperforms that of conventional Gaussian pulses by an order of magnitude, without much difference in peak gate fidelity. These results establish a route towards robust single-qubit control in large-scale quantum processors, advancing the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Adiabatic controlled-$Z$ Gate For Neutral Atoms With F\"orster-enhanced Rydberg Dressing
authors: Ajay Wasan Diksha Thapliyal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an adiabatic controlled-[MATH] (CZ) gate for neutral atoms in which dipole-dipole coupling between nearly degenerate Rydberg pair states enhances the interaction between dressed ground states. This coupling produces an avoided crossing in the two-atom dressed-state spectrum. Approaching the crossing enhances the dressed interaction, but also reduces the dressed-state gap and increases the Rydberg admixture. We identify a F\"orster-enhanced operating range in which the required conditional phase is accumulated with adiabatic return and small transient Rydberg population. We then analyze the finite-time dynamics of the two-qubit computational states under a smooth pulse. Reducing the dressing strength weakens the dressed interaction, so maintaining the target phase at the same pulse duration requires operation closer to the avoided crossing, where the Rydberg admixture increases. This dependence is then used to select the shortest gate at a fixed peak Rabi frequency in the F\"orster-enhanced operating range that accumulates the CZ phase with high Bell-state fidelity while keeping the Rydberg population small. Changing the F\"orster defect shifts the avoided crossing, while the gate parameters change only weakly. For a specific rubidium F\"orster channel, the selected gate corresponds to experimentally relevant laser coupling, pulse duration, and interatomic separation. We also estimate errors from the finite Rydberg lifetime and from weak excitation of a neighboring spectator atom. For the parameters considered, the spectator-induced error remains below the finite-lifetime contribution.

title: Designing Robust Quantum Gates
authors: Marin Bukov Yuanxing Hao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For given control channels, quantum control theory determines whether quantum gates can be realized, but not their resilience to errors. We address this problem by establishing existence criteria for robust gate implementation in [MATH]-level systems. Our criteria reveal that implementability of all gates is not enough: a universal family of robust gates exists if and only if the driven Hamiltonians share no common symmetry. When these criteria hold, we can make gates resilient to any combination of static perturbations, uniform Hamiltonian rescaling, perturbations at a finite set of selected frequencies, and perturbations with arbitrary selected waveforms. We can impose robustness conditions broadly with limited information about errors, e.g., against any static perturbations; we can also tailor these conditions to the platform, e.g., against environment-induced noise with dominant spectral peaks, requiring no spectral details beyond the peak frequencies. We numerically construct explicit protocols for robust gates, reducing average gate infidelity by approximately two to seven orders of magnitude under Hamiltonian perturbations and environment-induced noise. Together, our existence criteria and numerical constructions provide practical guidance for evaluating the potential of quantum platforms and designing robust quantum gates.
tldr: The paper establishes symmetry-based existence criteria for robust universal quantum gate implementation and numerically constructs control protocols resilient to broad Hamiltonian and environmental perturbations.
motivation: Quantum control theory can determine whether gates are realizable for given control channels, but it does not guarantee resilience to errors, leaving a gap for practical robust gate design.
method: The authors derive existence criteria for robust gate implementation in finite-level systems and construct explicit numerical protocols that impose robustness against static perturbations, uniform Hamiltonian rescaling, selected-frequency perturbations, arbitrary waveforms, and environment-induced noise.
result: A universal family of robust gates exists if and only if the driven Hamiltonians share no common symmetry; the constructed protocols reduce average gate infidelity by roughly two to seven orders of magnitude under Hamiltonian perturbations and noise.
conclusion: The work provides practical criteria and numerical guidance for evaluating quantum platforms and designing robust quantum gates with limited error information.

title: Generalized Svetlichny Inequalities As A Cross-Platform Benchmark For Quantum Processors
authors: Andr\'es Camilo Granda Arango, Giuseppe Sergioli, Luigi Iapichino, Tobias Valentin Bauer, Carlo Cuccu, Roberto Giuntini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A cross-platform benchmark should be device-independent yet sensitive to imperfections accumulated during execution. title: Local Response Theory Of Multiparameter Sudden-quench Quantum Otto Engines
authors: Dehua Liu, Yihang Cai, Biao Xiong, Jibing Liu, Chuanjia Shan, Jianhui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiparameter quantum Otto engines raise an optimization problem absent in single-parameter cycles: which small quench vector maximizes the quadratic approximation to the exact output work in a multidimensional control space? We develop a local response theory for sudden-quench Otto engines with quantum working media described by linearly controlled Hamiltonians. We show that the local quadratic work decomposes into a thermal-bias gain and a quadratic response cost, whose competition determines the quench vector that maximizes the local quadratic work at a prescribed quench amplitude. We illustrate the theory in a minimal two-level working medium, where radial and transverse quenches play distinct roles, and in a finite interacting XYZ spin chain, where the resulting quench vector is determined by the balance between thermal-bias and response cost. Our results provide a practical local criterion for designing small multiparameter quenches in sudden-quench quantum Otto engines.

method: They derive a local quadratic expansion of the exact output work for linearly controlled Hamiltonians, decomposing it into a thermal-bias gain and a quadratic response cost. The theory is illustrated with a two-level working medium and a finite interacting XYZ spin chain.
result: The optimal quench vector at fixed amplitude is determined by the competition between thermal-bias gain and response cost, with radial and transverse quenches playing distinct roles in the two-level case and a nontrivial balance emerging in the spin-chain example.
conclusion: The local response framework gives a practical criterion for designing small multiparameter quenches in sudden-quench quantum Otto engines and clarifies how control-space geometry affects work optimization.

title: Collective Strong Quantum Mpemba Effect In Accelerated Quantum Detectors
authors: G. D. de Moraes Neto, Richard Q. Matos, Norton G. de Almeida
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective coupling to the Minkowski vacuum allows uniformly accelerated quantum detectors to exhibit a strong quantum Mpemba effect, in which a state initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than a closer one. We establish the existence of this effect for every fixed finite number of detectors [MATH] at sufficiently small transverse separation within the pointlike secular master equation. The mechanism originates from two reflection sectors whose populations are conserved by the leading collective dynamics. Weak intersector transfer at finite separation generates an isolated, parametrically slow relaxation mode. A simple family of initial states permits its leading-order cancellation by matching the equilibrium sector populations, while a corrected preparation eliminates the slow-mode amplitude exactly. We construct a reference state that establishes a genuine reversal of trace-distance ordering. Numerical calculations and local-rate-preserving controls identify the collective origin of the effect, while spatially smeared detector calculations support its persistence within the second-order secular framework. The same mechanism extends to detectors coupled to a common thermal field, with analytically distinct slow relaxation rates. Thus, strong Mpemba relaxation is not exclusive to acceleration but emerges from a more general interplay between collective dissipation, reflection-sector conservation, and weak symmetry-breaking transfer.

authors: Yun Shang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum decoding succeeds when a correction matches the logical class of the error, whereas ordered-statistics decoding (OSD) searches a finite list of physical corrections. For fixed, error-independent orderings it yields the exact logical-signature distribution, the OSD-0 logical error rate, and the logical-class coverage of any fixed list. For minimum-cost list decoding we prove [MATH], separating absent-class from wrong-selection failures. Hypergraph-product and bivariate-bicycle codes are consistent with the coverage predictions. On the [MATH] gross code, 672 coverage-aware candidates outperform 899 combination-sweep candidates (paired McNemar [MATH]), while two lists with identical logical coverage give [MATH] and [MATH]; the signature-based coverage compression persists across 30 random column orderings. Logical coverage and within-class representative selection are therefore complementary resources that candidate count alone does not capture. The framework guides OSD list construction and compression by identifying coverage requirements and distinguishing coverage losses from failures of representative selection.

title: Concatenated Continuous-drive Protection Of Exchange-based Spin-qubit Gates
authors: Takuma Kuno, Takeru Utsugi, Andrew J. Ramsay, Hideo Arimoto, Tetsuo Kodera, Hiroyuki Mizuno
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exchange-based two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits are sensitive to low-frequency detuning noise and control errors. Here, we extend concatenated continuous driving (CCD), implemented by phase modulation of a global microwave drive, to exchange-based SWAP and [MATH] operations between double-dressed spin qubits and investigate its effectiveness for protecting two-qubit gates. We find that CCD retains strong protection against quasistatic common-mode detuning errors while substantially improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and qubit-to-qubit Rabi-frequency mismatch compared with conventional continuous dressing. By contrast, the gate fidelity is impacted by differential detuning errors. By modeling partially correlated quasistatic detuning noise, we further show that the noise-averaged gate fidelity depends strongly on the spatial correlation of the qubit-frequency fluctuations, with positive correlations enhancing CCD protection by suppressing the differential-noise component. These results identify the symmetry and spatial correlation of qubit-frequency noise as key factors governing continuous-drive protection in coupled spin-qubit systems.

motivation: Exchange-based two-qubit gates in spin qubits are highly sensitive to low-frequency detuning noise and control errors, motivating robust continuous-drive protection schemes.
method: The authors model concatenated continuous driving implemented by phase modulation of a global microwave drive and evaluate noise-averaged gate fidelity under quasistatic common-mode and differential detuning noise, Rabi-frequency errors, and qubit-to-qubit mismatch.
result: CCD retains strong protection against common-mode detuning while improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and mismatch compared with conventional continuous dressing, but differential detuning still degrades fidelity; positively correlated noise enhances protection by suppressing the differential component.
conclusion: The symmetry and spatial correlation of qubit-frequency noise are key factors governing continuous-drive protection in coupled spin-qubit systems.

The authors model the system with quasistatic detuning noise and Rabi-frequency errors, and evaluate gate fidelity through numerical simulations. They find that CCD maintains strong protection against common-mode detuning noise while significantly improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and qubit-to-qubit Rabi-frequency mismatch compared to conventional continuous dressing. However, differential detuning errors degrade fidelity. By modeling partially correlated noise, they show that the noise-averaged fidelity depends strongly on the spatial correlation of qubit-frequency fluctuations, with positive correlations enhancing CCD protection by suppressing the differential-noise component. The results highlight the importance of noise symmetry and spatial correlation in continuous-drive protection for coupled spin-qubit systems.

title: Probing Wetting And Solidification Dynamics Of Neon Thin Films With A high-$T_c$ Superconducting Circuit
authors: Brennan Dizdar, Yueheng Shi, David I. Schuster, Christopher S. Lang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating condensed noble gases with superconducting circuits offers new opportunities for operating hybrid quantum devices. In particular, electrons on solid neon have recently emerged as exceptionally coherent charge qubits, however the growth of the underlying neon films on patterned devices remains poorly controlled. We monitor neon films near the triple point using a multimode resonator fabricated from high-[MATH] YBCO, which remains superconducting at temperatures where the liquid phase exists and whose geometry sets a thickness-sensing window near 1 [MATH]m. In the liquid state we observe rich film dynamics: uniform wetting that saturates near 20 nm, drainage of thicker films, and spontaneous thickness oscillations, reflecting the extreme sensitivity of thick films in this regime. A galvanic connection to our sensing volume enables in-situ electrostatic tuning of the liquid film thickness. Statistics of freezing the neon across various liquid levels reveal variations of the solid film thickness by approximately an order of magnitude. We also observe a two-fold increase in the quality factor of the resonators at the level of [MATH] with added neon and rule out dielectric loss as the limiting factor. Our results demonstrate that hermetic packaging facilitates the investigation of both rich non-equilibrium fluid dynamics and the impact of condensed noble gas films on microwave loss in superconducting circuits, but may not be the best modality for growing solid neon films with precisely controlled thickness.
tldr: The paper uses a high-Tc YBCO superconducting multimode resonator to monitor wetting and solidification dynamics of neon thin films near the triple point, relevant to electrons-on-solid-neon hybrid quantum devices.
motivation: Electrons on solid neon are promising charge qubits, but controlled growth of neon films on patterned superconducting devices remains poorly understood.
method: A multimode YBCO resonator with a thickness-sensing window near 1 micron is used to track neon film thickness in liquid and solid states, with electrostatic tuning via a galvanic connection.
result: The authors observe rich liquid-film dynamics including uniform wetting up to ~20 nm, drainage, and spontaneous thickness oscillations; freezing produces solid-film thickness variations of about an order of magnitude, and adding neon increases resonator quality factor twofold without dielectric loss being limiting.
conclusion: Hermetic packaging enables studies of non-equilibrium fluid dynamics and microwave loss from condensed noble gases, but may not be ideal for growing solid neon films with precisely controlled thickness.

title: Nonlocality As A Benchmarking Tool For Quantum Processors
authors: Andr\'es Camilo Granda Arango, Carla Sophie Rieger, Carlo Cuccu, Giuseppe Sergioli, Luigi Iapichino, Tobias Valentin Bauer, Roberto Giuntini, Federico Hern\'an Holik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarking quantum processors is a central task in every roadmap aimed at quantum advantage. Here, we discuss a benchmarking protocol based on the violation of the Svetlichny inequality, which is designed to simulate genuine multipartite nonlocality. We compare it with Mermin's inequality, and present the results of applying this framework to two different quantum processing units -the superconducting system Garnet (from IQM) and the ion-trap system Marmot (from AQT), testing different families of quantum circuits for three to five qubits under identical experimental conditions. We also run simultaneous triplet tests across the full register, including a comparison between GHZ and linear cluster states, to probe how Svetlichny-inequality violations depend on qubit location and calibration. Our results demonstrate that tests based on genuine multipartite nonlocality provide a powerful tool to characterize the collective performance of quantum devices and to guide their calibration and optimization.
tldr: The paper proposes a benchmarking protocol for quantum processors based on violations of the Svetlichny inequality to probe genuine multipartite nonlocality.
motivation: Benchmarking quantum processors is essential for assessing progress toward quantum advantage, and nonlocality tests may provide a device-independent or collective-performance characterization tool.
method: The authors compare Svetlichny- and Mermin-inequality-based benchmarks and apply them to a superconducting IQM Garnet processor and an ion-trap AQT Marmot processor using three- to five-qubit circuit families, including GHZ and linear cluster states and simultaneous triplet tests across the register.
result: They find that genuine multipartite nonlocality violations can characterize collective device performance and reveal dependence on qubit location and calibration across the two hardware platforms.
conclusion: Nonlocality-based tests are argued to be a useful benchmarking tool for quantum processors and for guiding calibration and optimization.

title: Beyond Low-dissipation Regime: General Condition For Curzon-Ahlborn Efficiency
authors: Yuki Izumida
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, physicists have extensively investigated the universality of Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) efficiency as the efficiency at maximum power of heat engines, which, like Carnot efficiency, is determined only by heat-bath temperatures. While the universality of the CA efficiency to the first order in the temperature difference is established within linear response theory in the inverse operation time, it is generally lost at quadratic order. In the low-dissipation Carnot heat engine model known as the standard framework, the symmetric dissipation condition is necessary. Yet, it is not a necessary condition as the original CA model that adopts endoreversibility does not require such symmetry. In this study, we extend the low-dissipation model to include nonlinear response in the inverse operation time and derive a general condition under which the CA efficiency is recovered in the quadratic order. The generalized symmetric dissipation condition and the CA model with Newton's law of cooling are shown to be special cases of this condition. By applying the obtained condition, we also clarify the condition under which an endoreversible model with a general heat-transfer law exhibits the CA efficiency.
tldr: The paper derives a general condition under which heat engines operating at maximum power attain Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency at quadratic order in the temperature difference, extending the low-dissipation model beyond linear response.
motivation: Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency is universal at linear order but its quadratic-order validity is generally lost, and the known symmetric-dissipation condition from the low-dissipation model is sufficient but not necessary, as the original endoreversible CA model shows.
method: The low-dissipation Carnot heat engine model is generalized to include nonlinear response in the inverse operation time, and a general condition for recovering CA efficiency at quadratic order is derived analytically.
result: The generalized symmetric dissipation condition and the CA model with Newton's law of cooling emerge as special cases, and the framework clarifies when endoreversible models with arbitrary heat-transfer laws exhibit CA efficiency.
conclusion: CA efficiency's universality at quadratic order follows from a broader structural condition on dissipation and heat transfer, unifying previously separate low-dissipation and endoreversible derivations.

title: Asymmetric Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes
authors: Ramakrishna Bandi Vijay Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Locally recoverable codes (LRCs) permit reconstruction of a lost coordinate from a small subset of the remaining coordinates, a property that is a fundamental coding technique for distributed storage and, more recently, for fault-tolerant quantum memories and distributed storage systems. Existing constructions of quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) and their entanglement-assisted generalizations (EA-qLRCs) impose a single locality parameter [MATH] governing recovery from both bit-flip ([MATH]-type) and phase-flip ([MATH]-type) errors, even though physical noise is rarely symmetric between the two. We introduce entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EA-qLRC) with [MATH], in which [MATH]-type and [MATH]-type errors are corrected from recovery sets of size at most [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. We extend a stabilizer sufficient condition for this property and, in particular, the CSS framework, where asymmetric locality corresponds to separate locality conditions on the two classical codes [MATH] and [MATH] underlying the construction. From this characterization we derive Singleton-, Griesmer-, Plotkin-, sphere-packing-, and Cadambe\textendash Mazumdar-like bounds for CSS-type asymmetric EA-qLRCs (AEA-qLRCs) built from Proposition~, and we characterize exactly when a pure CSS-type AEA-qLRC built from a pair of classical LRCs attains the Singleton-like bound with equality.

motivation: Physical noise is often asymmetric between bit-flip and phase-flip errors, but existing quantum locally recoverable codes impose a single locality parameter, limiting efficiency for fault-tolerant quantum memories and distributed storage.
method: Extends a stabilizer sufficient condition and the CSS framework to asymmetric locality by imposing separate locality constraints on the two underlying classical LRCs, then derives Singleton-, Griesmer-, Plotkin-, sphere-packing-, and Cadambe-Mazumdar-like bounds.

conclusion: Asymmetric locality can improve quantum locally recoverable codes under realistic asymmetric noise, though the contribution is a specialized coding-theoretic advance rather than a core entanglement or information-theoretic result.

title: Operational Meaning Of The Mandelstam-Tamm Time Scale In A Spin-1/2 Clock
authors: Rog Jakub (james)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Georgiev's analysis of a freely precessing spin correctly emphasizes that the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity [MATH] is not the variance of a time operator. He concludes, however, that its divergence near the extrema of the clock signal is devoid of physical meaning and that [MATH] does not disclose how well the system measures the passage of time. For the same projective [MATH] readout, we show that [MATH] equals the inverse square root of the classical Fisher information in one binary outcome at regular operating points. Its divergence at submaximal-coherence extrema therefore identifies a loss of local sensitivity in the selected readout, not an infinite variance of physical time; a complementary [MATH] measurement remains informative. This interpretation also separates Georgiev's exactly known tick--tock period from the statistical precision with which a tick can be located. It preserves his warning against a time-operator interpretation while qualifying his stronger conclusion that the Mandelstam--Tamm scale lacks physical content.
tldr: The paper gives an operational interpretation of the Mandelstam-Tamm time scale in a spin-1/2 clock by linking it to classical Fisher information for a projective readout.
motivation: Georgiev argued that the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity diverges near clock-signal extrema and therefore lacks physical meaning as a time-measurement precision. This work re-examines that conclusion using an information-theoretic readout perspective.
method: For a freely precessing spin-1/2 clock with projective readout, the authors compare the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity with the classical Fisher information of a binary outcome at regular operating points and near extrema.
result: At regular operating points the Mandelstam-Tamm scale equals the inverse square root of the classical Fisher information, while its divergence at submaximal-coherence extrema signals loss of local sensitivity in the chosen readout rather than infinite temporal variance.
conclusion: The Mandelstam-Tamm scale retains operational meaning as a readout-dependent precision scale, while the warning against interpreting it as a time-operator variance remains valid.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper is a comment on Georgiev's analysis (Symmetry 16, 100 (2024)) of the Mandelstam-Tamm (MT) time-energy uncertainty relation applied to a freely precessing spin. Georgiev argued that the MT quantity ΔT = ΔÂ/|d⟨Â⟩/dt| is not a time-operator variance and that its divergence near the extrema of the clock signal (where the expectation value of the measured observable has zero derivative) is devoid of physical meaning, concluding that ΔT does not quantify how well the system measures time. The present authors challenge this stronger conclusion by showing that, for the same projective σ_x readout, ΔT equals the inverse square root of the classical Fisher information (FI) for one binary outcome at regular operating points. Consequently, the divergence at submaximal-coherence extrema reflects a loss of local sensitivity in the chosen readout, not an infinite variance of physical time. They note that a complementary σ_y measurement remains informative at those points. The authors also distinguish Georgiev's exactly known tick-tock period from the statistical precision with which a tick can be located, preserving his warning against interpreting ΔT as a time operator while qualifying his claim that the MT scale lacks physical content.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt a focused analytical approach: they consider a freely precessing spin (a two-level system) and the projective measurement of σ_x, which serves as the clock signal. They compute the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity ΔT = Δσ_x / |d⟨σ_x⟩/dt| and compare it to the classical Fisher information for a binary outcome. The Fisher information for a single binary outcome with probability p is F = (dp/dθ)^2 / [p(1-p)], where θ is the parameter to be estimated (here, time). By identifying the parameter as time and using the precession dynamics, they show that ΔT equals 1/√F at regular operating points. This establishes a direct link between the MT scale and the statistical precision of time estimation via the chosen readout. The analysis is straightforward and does not involve complex numerical simulations; it relies on exact expressions for the spin expectation values and their derivatives. The authors also discuss the behavior at extrema, where d⟨σ_x⟩/dt = 0, causing ΔT to diverge, and they argue that this divergence corresponds to F → 0 for that readout, indicating a loss of local sensitivity. They then note that a complementary σ_y measurement would have nonzero Fisher information at those points, demonstrating that the system still carries temporal information accessible via a different observable.

At the extrema of the clock signal (where ⟨σ_x⟩ reaches its maximum or minimum), the derivative vanishes, so F_class = 0 and ΔT diverges. The authors interpret this divergence as a loss of local sensitivity: the readout cannot distinguish small changes in time near the extrema because the signal is flat. This is a standard feature of parameter estimation and does not imply that time itself has infinite uncertainty. Furthermore, they show that at these extrema, a complementary σ_y measurement has nonzero Fisher information, so the system still provides a clock signal if one switches the readout. The paper does not provide numerical values but relies on exact analytical expressions. The results are qualitative in the sense that they reinterpret known quantities, but the identification with Fisher information is exact and provides a clear physical meaning to ΔT.

title: FTWeave: Composing Logical Execution, Real-Time Decoding, And Magic-State Supply In Tightly Integrated Quantum-Classical Systems
authors: Panayiotis Christou, Shuwen Kan, Ying Mao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum applications depend on both decoded measurement information and a continuing supply of magic states. While an operation waits for either, its logical data require protection that produces more syndrome data and decoding work. Architects must provision the quantum and classical parts of the machine together, before complete systems are available to measure. FTWeave is a system-level simulator for this architectural exploration. It accepts OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q Logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through adapters that preserve operation and measurement dependencies. Users bind these inputs to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations. One event timeline determines application progress, resource ownership, and continuing protection. This supplies the system model needed to connect circuit and decoder evidence to application performance. Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions. A fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from additional factories where the coupled model gives almost none. Explicit ownership also changes useful capacity: increasing decoder workers alone has no benefit in a storage-constrained case, while increasing workers and feedback entries together gives 4.93x speedup. Selected color and hypergraph-product code mappings take 53-90% longer under decoder service variability, despite an unchanged mean. These comparisons identify useful resource combinations and distinguish protection work from the elapsed lifetime of quantum data.
tldr: FTWeave is a system-level simulator that jointly models logical execution, real-time syndrome decoding, and magic-state factory supply to expose how quantum and classical resource provisioning interact in fault-tolerant architectures.
motivation: Fault-tolerant applications need both decoded measurement outcomes and a steady stream of magic states, and waiting on either resource generates additional syndrome data and decoding load; architects therefore need to co-provision quantum and classical hardware before full systems exist.
method: The tool ingests OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through dependency-preserving adapters, letting users bind them to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations on a single event timeline.
result: Controlled demand studies and full multiplier and Ising circuits show that a fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from extra factories where the coupled model shows almost none; scaling decoder workers plus feedback entries together yields 4.93x, and selected color/hypergraph-product code mappings run 53-90% longer under decoder service variability at unchanged mean.
conclusion: Coupling decoding, protection, and magic-state supply in one model materially changes provisioning decisions and distinguishes useful resource combinations from misleading single-resource scaling arguments.

title: EntangledEdge: A Distributed System For Orbital Quantum Sensing And Learning
authors: Mohammad Abrarul Hasanat, Amit Samanta, Jason Ludmir, Tirthak Patel, Rohan Basu Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An orbital quantum sensor is more precise than classical and holds its information in a quantum state's superposition and entanglement, which classical measurement collapses. Learning on quantum-sensed data therefore requires a distributed system in which the data stay quantum from sensor to inference. We present EntangledEdge, the first system architecture to unify orbital quantum sensing and learning end-to-end, with a quantum data plane and a classical control plane. It routes each event to a channel-matched model in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts its detection threshold without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity. Evaluated with a hybrid prototype (real quantum processors, simulated orbit-to-ground link) over satellite telemetry, EntangledEdge achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.
tldr: EntangledEdge is a distributed system architecture that keeps orbital quantum-sensor data quantum through to inference using a quantum data plane and classical control plane.
motivation: Orbital quantum sensors offer precision beyond classical sensors, but learning on their data requires preserving quantum states across sensing, communication, and inference rather than collapsing them into classical measurements.
method: The system routes events to channel-matched models in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts detection thresholds without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity; it is evaluated with a hybrid prototype using real quantum processors and a simulated orbit-to-ground link over satellite telemetry.
result: The prototype achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.
conclusion: The work proposes an end-to-end distributed architecture for orbital quantum sensing and learning, but its focus is applied systems engineering rather than core quantum network theory or entanglement distribution.

title: Characterizing Local And Correlated Pauli Noise In Quantum Teleportation Circuits
authors: L. Anjos, Jose Alfredo de Leon, R. S. Sarthour, Alejandro Fonseca
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analytically characterize how the location and the local or correlated structure of stochastic Pauli errors affect a three-qubit coherent quantum-teleportation circuit. Independent local channels and a fully correlated two-qubit channel are inserted separately in six configurations. Propagating each Pauli-error realization through the Clifford circuit yields the effective channel on Bob's qubit and analytical expressions for the average and state-resolved fidelities. Under a common ordered-pair probability convention, the six configurations form three pairs that induce equivalent reduced channels on Bob. Within each pair, corresponding Pauli-error realizations have the same probabilities and produce the same effective Pauli operator on Bob's output state. The equivalence therefore holds for every input state within the stochastic Pauli models considered here, rather than only for the average fidelity. Correlated Z errors do not affect the output for the first pair; local X and Z errors exhibit complementary qubit sensitivity for the second; and correlated same-axis Pauli errors cancel for the third. These results classify the error response of the selected circuit configurations and show that it depends jointly on the error statistics, Pauli axis, and position within the protocol.
tldr: The paper analytically characterizes how the position and local versus correlated structure of stochastic Pauli errors affect a three-qubit coherent quantum teleportation circuit.
motivation: Understanding how noise location and correlations propagate through teleportation circuits is important for assessing the reliability of near-term quantum information protocols.
method: Independent local Pauli channels and a fully correlated two-qubit channel are inserted in six configurations; each error realization is propagated through the Clifford circuit to obtain the effective channel on Bob's qubit along with analytical average and state-resolved fidelities.
result: Under a common ordered-pair probability convention the six configurations collapse into three equivalent pairs, with matching probabilities and identical effective Pauli operators on Bob's output for every input state; correlated Z errors vanish in one pair, local X/Z errors show complementary sensitivity in another, and same-axis correlated errors cancel in the third.
conclusion: The error response of the circuit depends jointly on error statistics, Pauli axis, and error position, providing a classification of noise sensitivity for these teleportation circuit configurations.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm For Mixed-State Quantum Geometry
authors: Chenyang Wang, Qi Zhao, Xiao Yuan, Xiaoxia Cai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed-state quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in quantum metrology, multiparameter estimation, and the characterization of quantum many-body systems. Yet, unlike its pure-state counterpart, accessing mixed-state geometry requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation for the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD), posing a major challenge for resource-efficient quantum computation. Here we address the challenge and develop a novel quantum algorithmic framework for efficiently accessing the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) and quantum geometric tensor (QGT) of mixed states. Our key insight is to uncover a previously unexplored connection between the positive semidefinite structure of density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, enabling an efficient integral-based construction of the SLD. A rigorous complexity analysis further establishes the resource efficiency of our algorithm, demonstrating logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancillary-qubit overhead at fixed conditioning. Building on this construction, we achieve near-Heisenberg precision scaling for diagonal QFI estimation without quantum phase estimation and construct unified block encodings of the full QFIM and QGT under a bounded spectral-gap assumption. A complementary regularized algorithm extends efficient diagonal estimation to exponentially small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition. Our results establish a resource-efficient route to coherent mixed-state quantum geometry, enabling its direct integration into quantum linear-algebra algorithms without classical reconstruction and opening new possibilities for quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.
tldr: The paper proposes an efficient quantum algorithmic framework for computing the quantum Fisher information matrix and quantum geometric tensor of mixed states.
motivation: Mixed-state quantum geometry is important for metrology and many-body characterization, but its central object, the symmetric logarithmic derivative, requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation.
method: The authors exploit a connection between positive semidefinite density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature to construct the SLD, then build block encodings and a regularized estimator for the QFIM and QGT.
result: The algorithm achieves logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancilla overhead at fixed conditioning, near-Heisenberg scaling for diagonal QFI, and efficient diagonal estimation for small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition.
conclusion: The work provides a resource-efficient coherent route to mixed-state quantum geometry that can be integrated into quantum linear-algebra algorithms and quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.

title: Trajectree - A Quantum Trajectory-based Quantum Circuit Simulator
authors: Ansh Singal, Allen Zang, Jordan Thomas, Alexander Kolar, Anirudh Ramesh, Joaquin Chung, Rajkumar Kettimuthu, Prem Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Trajectree, a quantum trajectory-based quantum circuit simulator that uses a novel, state-saving partial execution of the quantum circuits to simulate broad and deep noisy quantum circuits efficiently. Trajectree can efficiently generate a large number of Monte Carlo samples by saving partially executed trajectories. We conduct extensive performance analysis of the Trajectree approach, proving the utility of the trajectory saving scheme for simulations of open quantum systems. Using this architecture, we show that Trajectree can simulate standard benchmark noisy circuits over five times faster than Google's QSim, a part of the Cirq package. We also analyze Trajectree's performance for simulating quantum optical systems relevant to communication and computing applications. We demonstrate applications of the optical backend to simulate three optical experiments: CHSH Bell test, entanglement swapping, and optical CNOT gate. This shows Trajectree's potential for simulating noisy qudit and optical systems efficiently.
tldr: Trajectree is a quantum-trajectory-based circuit simulator that saves partially executed trajectories to efficiently sample noisy quantum circuits and optical systems.
motivation: Simulating broad and deep noisy quantum circuits efficiently is challenging, especially when many Monte Carlo trajectory samples are needed for open-system and optical experiments.
method: The simulator performs state-saving partial execution of quantum circuits, reusing partially executed trajectories to generate many Monte Carlo samples, and includes an optical backend for simulating photonic experiments.
result: Trajectree simulates standard noisy-circuit benchmarks over five times faster than Google's QSim and is demonstrated on CHSH Bell tests, entanglement swapping, and an optical CNOT gate.
conclusion: The work provides a practical simulation tool for noisy qudit and optical systems, with potential utility for quantum communication and computing applications, though its main contribution is computational performance rather than quantum information theory.

title: Exact Quantum Query Complexity Of The Five-Bit Symmetric Boolean Function $\Exact^5_{3,4}$
authors: Guoliang Xu, Haoran Zhang, Mengfan Wu, Songyao Xue, Mingke Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let \(f = ^5_{3,4}\) be the Boolean function that equals 1 exactly on inputs of Hamming weight 3 or 4. Earlier numerical studies reported success probabilities close to one using three queries, but the existence of an exact three-query algorithm had remained unresolved. This paper settles this problem by proving that the exact quantum query complexity of \(f\) is \(4\). For the lower bound, we express every three-query algorithm through layer-by-layer Gram matrices of low-degree Fourier coefficients. We then construct a fixed rational dual certificate whose slack matrices are all positive definite. This certificate separates the necessary Gram-matrix region from the exact-output condition and therefore rules out every exact algorithm using at most three queries in the stated model. The positivity verification reduces to five small rational matrices and Sylvester's criterion. For the upper bound, we invoke the previously known four-query algorithm for the seven-bit function \(^7_{3,4}\) and apply the standard padding reduction. To quantify the near-exact behavior, we use the same certificate to derive a valid, though not claimed tight, lower bound \({43779488192449}>0\) on the worst-case error of every algorithm using at most three queries. This positive error gap is compatible with the near-unit success probabilities reported in earlier numerical studies, which do not establish exact computation.
tldr: The paper proves that the exact quantum query complexity of the five-bit symmetric Boolean function Exact^5_{3,4} is 4, resolving a previously open three-query question.
motivation: Earlier numerical work suggested near-unit success with three queries, but whether an exact three-query quantum algorithm exists remained unresolved.
method: The lower bound uses layer-by-layer Gram matrices of low-degree Fourier coefficients and constructs a rational dual certificate with positive-definite slack matrices; the upper bound pads a known four-query algorithm for the seven-bit function.
result: Every exact algorithm requires at least four queries, while four queries suffice; the certificate also yields a positive lower bound on the worst-case error of any three-query algorithm.
conclusion: The exact quantum query complexity is settled as 4, and the positive error gap explains why numerical near-success probabilities do not imply exact computation.

title: Maximum-Temperature Theorem For A Nanothermometer
authors: Taras Plakhotnik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The steady-state temperature predicted for an ideal point heat source diverges in conventional heat-conduction theory, but no physical thermometer measures a point value. We derive a sharp, shape-independent upper bound on the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor with thermometric volume [MATH], placed anywhere inside a region enclosed by an isothermal reference surface. The bound requires only the total heat power generated in the region [MATH], a lower bound on its thermal conductivity [MATH], and the value of [MATH]. It is otherwise independent of the heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source--sensor distance. For [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], approximately the volume of a [MATH]-diameter sphere, the theorem permits a maximum temperature rise of approximately [MATH] above the reference level. The result applies directly to nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer particles, and core-shell quantum dots. It shows that neither source localization nor uncertain source-sensor separation can account for kelvin-scale readings under steady-state heat conduction.
tldr: The paper derives a shape-independent upper bound on the steady-state temperature rise measured by a nanoscale thermometer of finite thermometric volume.
motivation: Conventional heat-conduction theory predicts diverging temperatures for an ideal point heat source, but real nanothermometers measure a volume-averaged temperature, so a rigorous bound is needed that does not depend on unknown source geometry or source-sensor distance.
method: Using heat-conduction theory, the author bounds the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor volume placed inside an isothermal reference surface, requiring only the total heat power, a lower bound on thermal conductivity, and the thermometric volume.
result: The bound is independent of heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source-sensor separation; for realistic nanoscale parameters it permits only a limited temperature rise, implying that neither source localization nor uncertain separation can explain kelvin-scale readings under steady-state conduction.
conclusion: The theorem applies directly to nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer particles, and core-shell quantum dots, constraining interpretations of nanothermometry experiments based on steady-state heat conduction.

title: Prototype-Guided Optimization Of Quantum Data Embeddings With Linear Cost
authors: Daniel K. Park Seokhoon Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as [MATH] for [MATH] samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only [MATH] fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.
tldr: The paper proposes a prototype-guided framework to optimize quantum data embeddings with linear fidelity-evaluation cost for supervised quantum machine learning.
motivation: Existing data-adaptive quantum embedding methods rely on pairwise fidelities, scaling quadratically with sample count and creating a bottleneck for iterative optimization.
method: The authors use class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness to derive a distinguishability certificate and a prototype-based objective requiring only O(M) fidelity evaluations, integrated into an end-to-end pipeline with circuit architecture and embedding-parameter optimization.
result: Across five benchmark datasets up to 20 qubits, the method retains competitive quantum kernel SVM performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST.
conclusion: Prototype-guided embedding optimization offers a cost-efficient alternative for quantum kernel methods, though benefits are dataset-dependent and the work is primarily applied QML rather than information-theoretic.

title: BQP^cc Is Not Contained In MA^cc
authors: Dmytro Gavinsky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We exhibit a bipartite language with a poly-logarithmic quantum communication protocol and polynomial Merlin-Arthur communication complexity.
tldr: The paper separates quantum communication complexity from Merlin-Arthur communication complexity by constructing a bipartite language in BQP^cc but not in MA^cc.
motivation: Quantum communication complexity and classical interactive proof systems are natural models for comparing quantum and classical communication power, and this work addresses whether quantum protocols can outperform Merlin-Arthur communication.
method: The author proves a communication-complexity separation by exhibiting an explicit bipartite language with a polylogarithmic quantum communication protocol and polynomial Merlin-Arthur communication complexity.
result: The main result is that BQP^cc is not contained in MA^cc, establishing a new separation between quantum communication and classical Merlin-Arthur communication.
conclusion: This advances quantum communication complexity theory but lies outside the researcher's core interests in entanglement, nonlocality, entropy, cryptography, and thermodynamics.

title: A Self-Coupling Gaussian Extremal Inequality For Information-Constrained Optimal Transport With Applications To Rate-Distortion-Perception
authors: Jiayang Zou, Jun Chen, Ayfer \"{o}zg\"{u}r, Jia Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much mutual information is needed to achieve a target correlation between two copies of a prescribed distribution? We prove a sharp Gaussian extremal inequality for this self-coupling problem: among distributions with a fixed mean and covariance, the Gaussian has the greatest minimum information cost for meeting a positive semidefinite cross-covariance target. The inequality is strict for non-Gaussian distributions when the target is positive definite. The proof uses a midpoint gluing construction. Two Ornstein--Uhlenbeck half-bridges, each started from the prescribed endpoint law, meet at a common intermediate distribution and are joined by conditional gluing. Changing the Gaussian reference then turns the resulting relative-entropy bound into the desired extremal inequality. As a first application, scaling one endpoint of the self-coupling establishes Gaussian extremality for rate-distortion-perception with unlimited common randomness, under quadratic distortion and squared Wasserstein-2 perception measures. We also establish an analogous result for finite common randomness, where the problem involves two mutual information constraints associated with an auxiliary random variable. In that setting, we retain an intermediate observation on one half-bridge and balance the two information budgets simultaneously using the Poincar\'{e}-Miranda theorem.
tldr: The paper proves a sharp Gaussian extremal inequality for an information-constrained self-coupling problem and applies it to rate-distortion-perception with quadratic distortion and Wasserstein-2 perception.
motivation: The authors study how much mutual information is required to achieve a prescribed cross-covariance between two copies of a distribution, motivated by optimal transport and rate-distortion-perception trade-offs.
method: They use a midpoint gluing construction with two Ornstein-Uhlenbeck half-bridges joined by conditional gluing, converting a relative-entropy bound into a Gaussian extremal inequality; for finite common randomness they balance two information constraints via the Poincare-Miranda theorem.
result: Among distributions with fixed mean and covariance, the Gaussian maximizes the minimum information cost for positive semidefinite cross-covariance targets, with strictness for non-Gaussian laws when the target is positive definite; this yields Gaussian extremality for rate-distortion-perception with unlimited and finite common randomness.
conclusion: The work provides a sharp information-theoretic characterization of self-coupling costs and establishes Gaussian optimality in a rate-distortion-perception setting, but it is a classical information-theory result without direct quantum information content.

title: Don't Judge An Agent By Its Messages: Private-State Leakage Under Passive Monitoring Of Agent Communication
authors: Daksh Pandey, Sayon Duttagupta, Xinhai Zou, Amit Singh Bhati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An AI agent can reproduce the distribution of its messages and of the receiver's task outcomes while disclosing private information that the task never required. We ask what a passive audit can certify when the auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable law but has no trusted pairing of messages with the private states behind them. For a single round, compatible mutual-information leakage forms a sharp interval, and fixing the entire task-relevant message law, with every declared task utility, can still leave a full private bit undetermined; total leakage is determined if and only if, in every task state, the remaining private state or the authorised message is a deterministic function of that state. For a sender, such as an LLM, that selects among its own responses, we prove that in a balanced case its change to the message law within each task state equals [MATH] times the honest messages' dependence on the attribute, which also sets, up to a constant, how many messages a monitor needs. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a synthetic routing task, selection among 16 responses lets a public decoder recover a private bit in all 8,192 held-out rounds at 98.60\% routing accuracy (honest sender 98.90\%). A monitor that knows the selection rule reaches AUC 0.645 on single messages, close to the ceiling of 0.671 that honest messages predict, and 0.972 over 16, while generic monitors stay near chance. A law-preserving sender built from the same samples recovers the bit in 97.7\% of rounds, and every monitor without the true bit stays near chance against it. A canonical task interface preserves every receiver decision and bounds the remaining information about a balanced attribute by twice the routing-error rate, even for a receiver that shares a key with the sender. These results distinguish what passive auditing can certify from what restricting communication can enforce.
tldr: The paper characterizes what a passive auditor can certify about private-state leakage from an AI agent's messages when only the authorized message law is known, deriving sharp mutual-information intervals and validating them with Qwen2.5 experiments.
motivation: Agentic LLM deployments raise the question of whether message-level auditing can detect private information that a task never required, given that an agent can match the honest message distribution and task outcomes while still leaking.
method: Information-theoretic analysis of compatible mutual-information leakage for a single round under fixed task-relevant message laws, plus an operational bound for senders that select among their own responses, tested on a synthetic routing task with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and a public decoder/monitor.
