result: Leakage forms a sharp interval and can remain a full private bit even when the entire task-relevant law is fixed; empirically a decoder recovers the private bit in all 8,192 held-out rounds at 98.60% routing accuracy, with a rule-aware monitor reaching AUC 0.645 on single messages (ceiling 0.671) and 0.972 over 16.
conclusion: Passive auditing certifies strictly less than communication restriction can enforce; total leakage is determined only under determinism conditions, and a canonical task interface bounds residual information by twice the routing-error rate.

title: Margin-Based Generalization For Quantum Machine Learning With Classical Data Encoding
authors: Ju-Young Ryu, Tak Hur, Daniel K. Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order [MATH], where [MATH] is the number of trainable encoding parameters and [MATH] is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.
tldr: The paper develops margin-based generalization bounds for quantum machine learning models that encode classical data into quantum states, covering both fixed and trainable encodings and validating them across ~19,440 simulated training runs.
motivation: Generalization guarantees are needed to judge whether quantum machine learning models are practically viable, and since classical data must be embedded into quantum states, the encoding itself becomes part of the effective hypothesis class and must be accounted for in capacity bounds.
method: For fixed encodings the classical margin bound is shown to transfer unchanged; for trainable encodings a two-scale covering argument yields a bound combining the margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term scaling with the number of trainable encoding parameters over the sample size, tested against five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures on image datasets.
result: Across extensive simulations, the inverse margin outperforms alternative complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria within bootstrap uncertainty, though the encoding-capacity correction is additive and does not empirically dominate.
conclusion: The work offers a unified margin-based perspective on generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data encoding, but its contribution is statistical learning theory rather than quantum information theory.

title: Explicit Construction Of Optimal Binary Linear Complementary Pairs Via Belov Codes
authors: Yansheng Wu, Jing Chen, Jong Yoon Hyun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The study of linear complementary pairs (LCPs) has been a hot topic in coding theory. Recently, G\"uneri constructed an infinite family of optimal binary LCPs from Solomon-Stiffler codes. Specifically, he proved that for every [MATH] and [MATH], there exist optimal binary linear complementary pairs of codes of length [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the Griesmer bound. In this paper, we construct additional optimal binary LCPs from Belov codes, which form a generalized class of Solomon-Stiffler codes. Our results not only generalize G\"uneri's construction, but also enable more flexible construction of optimal binary LCPs with a wide range of minimum distances.
tldr: The paper explicitly constructs new infinite families of optimal binary linear complementary pairs (LCPs) of codes using Belov codes, generalizing Güneri's earlier Solomon-Stiffler-based construction.
motivation: Linear complementary pairs have attracted attention in coding theory (and in masking countermeasures against side-channel attacks), and previously only Solomon-Stiffler codes were known to yield optimal binary LCPs meeting the Griesmer bound for all admissible parameters.
method: Belov codes, a generalized class of Solomon-Stiffler codes obtained from a different geometric/linear-programming construction, are analyzed and shown to produce optimal binary LCPs; parameters and minimum distances are derived via the Griesmer bound.
result: The authors obtain additional optimal binary LCPs with a wider and more flexible range of lengths and minimum distances, strictly containing Güneri's family as a special case.
conclusion: Belov codes provide a strictly more general route to optimal binary LCPs, enlarging the known catalogue of such pairs and enabling more flexible parameter choices.

title: Pre-Query Retention With Bounded Bit And Word Retrieval
authors: Prashant Singh Pranav Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.
tldr: The paper studies how much fixed-length memory an agent must retain, alongside an immutable binary archive, to answer future queries under worst-case limits on bit or word reads.
motivation: Agents that must pre-encode possible records before knowing the query need retention schemes whose retrieval cost (response width) and storage are jointly characterized, which existing decision-tree capacity bounds do not address.
method: The authors characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells, construct encoders that partition the full record space, and combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse for multiple reads.
result: One-bit-read cells supporting XOR and AND suffice for all Boolean queries; for small read budgets word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits, and raw-word caching is exactly optimal under explicit conditions on word width and archive length, validated by exhaustive checks and a dialogue-agent study.
conclusion: Retention requirements are jointly determined by response width and future query structure, yielding tight characterizations in the bounded-read regime.

title: Where Should We Look For The Deviation From Quantum Mechanics?
authors: Albert Schwarz Jerome Nicolas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We argue that the experimental measurement of the lifetime and decay law of metastable helium is a promising way to find a deviation from quantum mechanics. We analyze the decay of the metastable state for a quartic deformation of quantum mechanics. We find that the absolute change of the mean lifetime can be significant even if the modification is small. We show that, in the Wigner--Weisskopf approximation, the deviation from the exponential law in the modified theory can occur on time scales comparable with the lifetime.
tldr: The authors propose measuring the lifetime and decay law of metastable helium as a probe for deviations from ordinary quantum mechanics predicted by a quartic deformation of the theory.
motivation: Experimental tests of whether quantum mechanics is exact are of foundational interest, but the paper motivates this mainly from a modified-quantum-mechanics perspective rather than from any information-theoretic or thermodynamic question.
method: They analyze the decay of a metastable state under a quartic deformation of quantum mechanics, computing the modified mean lifetime and, within the Wigner-Weisskopf approximation, the resulting non-exponential corrections to the decay law.
result: They find that the absolute change in mean lifetime can be significant even for small deformations, and that deviations from the exponential decay law can appear on timescales comparable to the lifetime itself.
conclusion: Metastable helium decay is argued to be a promising experimental window on deformations of quantum theory, though the work is a foundational/nuclear-physics proposal with no direct bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid platforms.

title: Comment On "The Polarization Hierarchy For Polynomial Optimization Over Convex Bodies, With Applications To Nonnegative Matrix Rank"
authors: Julius A. Zeiss
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the feasibility and convergence claims for the polarization hierarchy of Pl\'avala, Ligthart and Gross [Linear Algebra Appl.\ 723 (2025) 15--32]. Counterexamples show that the stated assumption is insufficient for the feasibility characterization and for convergence of the hierarchy with the polarization constraint. We establish corrected results under a stronger algebraic condition and supply a missing compactness argument.
tldr: A comment/correction paper revisiting the feasibility and convergence claims of the 'polarization hierarchy' for polynomial optimization over convex bodies.
motivation: The authors claim that the original polarization hierarchy paper (Plávala, Ligthart, Gross, LAA 2025) rests on an insufficient assumption, so its feasibility characterization and convergence guarantees need repair.
method: Counterexamples are constructed to show the stated assumption fails, then corrected results are derived under a stronger algebraic condition, together with a missing compactness argument.
result: The original feasibility characterization and convergence with the polarization constraint are shown to be invalid as stated; revised theorems hold only under the stronger condition.
conclusion: The polarization hierarchy remains viable but requires a stronger algebraic hypothesis and additional compactness reasoning for rigorous convergence.

title: Transient Heat Conduction On Quantum Hardware: Replicated Temperature-Field Reconstruction And Shot-Count Sensitivity With A Variational Quantum Linear Solver
authors: Yuwen Zhang Yijin Mao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Implicit discretizations of transient heat conduction repeatedly generate sparse linear systems, making diffusion problems a natural test bed for quantum linear solvers. This study evaluates how accurately a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) recovers the temperature field produced by one backward-Euler step of one-dimensional conduction on IBM quantum hardware. A pre-specified confirmatory experiment compares N=4 interior temperatures encoded on two qubits with N=8 temperatures encoded on three qubits using ten paired hardware blocks; a separately defined N=16, four-qubit extension is evaluated in five independently scheduled exploratory blocks. Local VQLS optimization reduces relative temperature-field error to approximately 10^{-8} for all three cases, establishing an essentially exact ideal reference at this scale. On hardware, mean relative L2 temperature-field error is 8.07% for N=4 and 20.14% for N=8, a paired increase of 12.06 percentage points (95% CI, 10.71-13.42; exact paired sign-flip p=0.001953). The exploratory N=16 mean is 24.75+/-1.84%. A pre-specified N=16 shot-count follow-up then evaluates the same locked circuit at 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 shots in six independently scheduled blocks. Mean field error remains 23.64%, 24.57%, and 24.37%, respectively; the 32,768-minus-2,048-shot contrast is +0.74 percentage points (95% CI, -0.65 to 2.12; p=0.281). In contrast, ideal multinomial sampling predicts a reduction from 2.68% to 0.75%. Higher shot counts reduce block-to-block variability but do not recover the mean cold-side temperature field. The results show that full-field readout of a strongly nonuniform thermal state is limited by more than ordinary finite-shot sampling under the tested hardware conditions, motivating observable-focused quantum formulations for heat flux, stored energy, and selected temperatures.
tldr: A hardware demonstration that a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) reproduces one backward-Euler step of 1D transient heat conduction, quantifying how temperature-field error grows with problem size and how it is not cured by more shots.
motivation: Implicit time-stepping of diffusion problems repeatedly produces sparse linear systems, making them an appealing benchmark for quantum linear solvers; the authors ask how accurately such solvers reconstruct a full nonuniform temperature field on real noisy hardware.
method: VQLS circuits encoding N=4 (2 qubits), N=8 (3 qubits) and N=16 (4 qubit) interior temperatures are run on IBM hardware in paired confirmatory blocks, with a pre-specified shot-count follow-up at 2048/8192/32768 shots and comparison against ideal multinomial sampling predictions.
result: Ideal local optimization reaches ~1e-8 relative error, but hardware mean relative L2 field errors are 8.07% (N=4), 20.14% (N=8) and 24.75% (N=16); increasing shots from 2048 to 32768 changes the mean error by only +0.74 percentage points (p=0.281) instead of the predicted drop from 2.68% to 0.75%.
conclusion: Full-field readout of strongly nonuniform thermal states on current hardware is limited by more than finite-shot statistics, suggesting observable-focused formulations (heat flux, stored energy, selected temperatures) rather than whole-field reconstruction.

title: Quantum-Correlation-Based Multi-Emitter Localization In Information-Limited Regimes Via Learned Inference
authors: Simeon I. Bogdanov Sanket K. Tripathy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum correlation measurements have emerged as a powerful tool for localizing multiple emitters with subwavelength separation. Multi-emitter localization consists of two distinct tasks: identifying the emitter count [MATH] and estimating their positions [MATH]. Existing fit-and-select frameworks fit the measured intensity and autocorrelation data using several models corresponding to different values of [MATH] and then select the best-supported model. This procedure lets errors from the multi-parameter optimization of emitter positions propagate into the choice of model, degrading performance under photon-limited and high-background conditions. We propose a method that directly infers the emitter count and positions from the multimodal data via learned inference. Learned inference improves both the emitter-counting accuracy and localization precision compared to the fit-and-select method. It achieves more than tenfold improvement in precision and requires up to five times fewer photons to achieve practically meaningful localization with the largest gains observed under low photon counts, strong background, narrowly spaced emitter configurations, and spatially truncated data. This photon-efficient quantum-assisted localization framework offers a promising route toward real-time biological imaging and single-particle tracking in densely labeled samples.
tldr: The paper uses learned inference on quantum correlation data to jointly estimate emitter count and positions for subwavelength multi-emitter localization in photon-limited regimes.
motivation: Existing fit-and-select methods suffer from error propagation between position fitting and model selection, especially under low photon counts and high background.
method: The authors replace the fit-and-select pipeline with a learned inference approach that directly maps multimodal intensity and autocorrelation data to emitter number and positions.
result: Learned inference improves emitter-counting accuracy and localization precision, achieving over tenfold precision improvement and requiring up to five times fewer photons, with the largest gains in low-photon, high-background, closely spaced, and truncated-data regimes.
conclusion: The framework provides a photon-efficient quantum-assisted localization method with potential for real-time biological imaging and single-particle tracking in densely labeled samples.

title: Siesta-qcomp: Bridging Classical And Quantum Computing For Strongly Correlated Systems
authors: Yann Pouillon, Federico Marchesin, Ivano Tavernelli, Emilio Artacho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the established workhorse of computational materials science, yet it faces fundamental challenges with strongly correlated electrons, such as in transition metal complexes and bond-breaking processes. While quantum computing offers a theoretically exact path to resolve these problems, current hardware limitations prohibit fully quantum simulations of realistic material systems. To bridge this gap, we present SIESTA-QCOMP, a modular suite embedding quantum methodologies within DFT. Harnessing SIESTA's localised basis set, we implement a projection-based embedding scheme that treats the bulk environment classically while mapping the strongly correlated "impurity" subspace to a quantum processor. The architecture uses a socket-based driver to orchestrate workflows between the Fortran-based SIESTA engine and Python-based frameworks like Qiskit, ensuring high interoperability. We detail the hybrid workflow, currently utilising a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and discuss the road map toward methods such as Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD). We illustrate the framework on an hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation and argue that such hybrid architectures are not merely interim solutions but essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design, as envisioned by our broader QCOMP4DFT initiative.
tldr: SIESTA-QCOMP is a modular classical-quantum workflow that embeds a strongly correlated impurity subspace from DFT into a quantum processor using VQE.
motivation: DFT struggles with strongly correlated electrons, while fully quantum simulations of realistic materials remain impractical on current hardware, motivating hybrid embedding approaches.
method: The framework combines SIESTA's localized-basis DFT engine with Python quantum frameworks such as Qiskit via a socket-based driver, using projection-based embedding to treat the environment classically and the impurity quantum mechanically with VQE.
result: The paper describes the architecture and illustrates it on a hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation, with a roadmap toward sample-based quantum diagonalization.
conclusion: The authors argue that such hybrid DFT-quantum architectures are essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design rather than merely interim solutions.

title: Realization Of Valley-controlled Orbital Angular Momentum Via Inter-orbital Coupling
authors: Wenxia Xu, Ziteng Wang, Yihan Wang, Qinggang Shang, Liqin Tang, Jingjun Xu, Hrvoje Buljan, Daohong Song, Zhigang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) represents a fundamental degree of freedom (DoF) for understanding novel phenomena in solids and synthetic lattices. However, the generation and control of OAM in lattice systems remain challenging. Here, we experimentally observe valley-controlled OAM states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices consisting of s- and higher-orbital sublattices. These OAM states manifest as chiral vortex arrays in real space. By selectively exciting s-orbital modes carrying no initial OAM at either the K or K' valley, we observe higher-orbital OAM modes generated via inter-orbital coupling in neighboring sites. Specifically, s-p orbital coupling generates OAM states with topological charge l=+1 or l=-1, while s-d orbital coupling yields higher-charge OAM states with l=+2 or l=-2. The sign of the topological charge is determined by the valley DoF, enabling deterministic control of vortex chirality across the entire array. Our theory further reveals that a local vortex-chirality symmetry enforces the valley-dependent selection of vortex chirality at the K and K' valleys, establishing a direct connection between the valley DoF and real-space vortex chirality. These results establish a versatile platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays via orbital physics and exploring orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena in photonic systems and beyond.
tldr: Experiments demonstrate valley-controlled orbital angular momentum (OAM) states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices, where inter-orbital s-p and s-d coupling converts valley-polarized excitation into chiral vortex arrays with topological charge l = ±1 or ±2.
motivation: OAM is a fundamental degree of freedom in solids and synthetic lattices, but generating and controlling OAM in lattice systems remains difficult; the authors aim to harness valley and orbital degrees of freedom to achieve deterministic, spatially extended control of vortex chirality.
method: Photonic honeycomb lattices with s- and higher-orbital sublattices are fabricated and probed by selectively exciting s-orbital modes at the K or K' valley; the resulting mode evolution and vortex structure are measured and compared with a tight-binding-type theory including a local vortex-chirality symmetry.
result: Inter-orbital coupling generates higher-orbital OAM modes with topological charge l = ±1 (s-p) and l = ±2 (s-d), with the charge sign fixed by the valley index, yielding deterministic chirality control across the whole array.
conclusion: The work establishes a versatile photonic platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays through orbital physics and links valley degrees of freedom to real-space vortex chirality, with potential relevance to orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena beyond photonics.

title: A Large Nonmagnetic aluminum-and-Viton Vacuum Chamber Suitable For Vacuum Pressures Down Into The Extremely-high-vacuum (xhv) Regime
authors: N. T. Mccall, H. -M. Yau, Z. Corriveau, J. Perez Garcia, T. Chauhan, G. K. Koyanagi, R. L. Lambo, M. C. George, C. H. Storry, E. A. Hessels
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recently constructed large nonmagnetic vacuum chamber is described and characterized. The vacuum chamber was machined from 19-inch cubes of aluminum and are sealed using dual Viton O-rings (with the interspace between the O-rings evacuated by a separate vacuum pump). 17-inch-diameter openings on all six sides allow for easy access to the experimental apparatus and for vacuum pumps with very large pumping speeds. These 17-inch holes were bored straight through the aluminum cube, resulting in an interior volume of 100 L (almost 90\% of the total volume of the 19-inch cube). The 17-inch openings are sealed with 19-inch-diameter aluminum flanges. The system is modular in that the cubes can be connected to one another to form larger vacuum systems. The chamber is designed to allow for vacuum pressures of [MATH] torr. In many respects (including nonmagnetic properties, outgassing rate after low-temperature baking, weight, cost, ease of machining, and ease of baking due to the chamber's high thermal conductivity) this system is superior to standard stainless-steel metal-sealed CF vacuum systems and is highly recommended for use by others.
tldr: The paper describes and characterizes a large nonmagnetic aluminum vacuum chamber sealed with dual Viton O-rings that reaches XHV pressures and is modular for scaling.
motivation: Standard stainless-steel CF vacuum systems are magnetic, heavy, expensive, and hard to bake; the authors seek a cheaper, lighter, nonmagnetic alternative suitable for precision atomic experiments requiring XHV.
method: 19-inch aluminum cubes are bored through with 17-inch openings on all six sides, sealed with dual Viton O-rings whose interspace is separately pumped, and characterized by outgassing and pressure measurements after low-temperature baking.
result: The modular chamber achieves an interior volume of 100 L (about 90% of the cube volume), supports very high pumping speeds and access via 19-inch flanges, and is designed for pressures in the XHV regime.
conclusion: The design is argued to outperform stainless-steel metal-sealed CF systems in nonmagnetic character, outgassing, weight, cost, machinability, and bakeability, and is recommended for broader use.

title: Boosting Fluorescence And Polarization With Nanophotonics For Single-molecule Chiral Sensing
authors: Ershad Mohammadi, T. V. Raziman, Alberto G. Curto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.
tldr: The paper proposes a reciprocity-based analytical framework to design high-index dielectric nanoantennas that simultaneously enhance fluorescence intensity (~1000x) and circular polarization contrast (~10x) for single-molecule chiral sensing.
motivation: Circular dichroism is too weak at low concentrations, and fluorescence-based chiral detection suffers from weak signals and low polarization contrast, so a route to single-molecule sensitivity is needed.
method: A reciprocity-based analytical model of a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanophotonic antenna is developed to separate fluorescence and polarization enhancement contributions and trade-offs, then used to tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures.
result: Tailored structures achieve 1000-fold fluorescence enhancement with 10-fold polarization increase, and the authors show that extrinsic polarization effects in angular emission patterns must be accounted for to reliably discriminate enantiomers.
conclusion: Dielectric nanophotonics offers a realistic path toward single-molecule chiral sensing, though the work is an optics/plasmonics design study rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics contribution.

title: Reusable QUBO-Derived Block-Schur Inverse Factors For Fixed-Operator Finite-Difference Pde Solvers
authors: Arash Fath Lipaei, \"ozg\"ur E. M\"ustecapl{\i}o\u{g}lu, \"ozlem Salehi, Selin Aslan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many simulations of partial differential equations require the repeated solution of linear systems whose matrix remains fixed while the righthand side changes. We present a hybrid offline online framework for this setting. The discretized operator is organized into small coupled blocks and reduced through block Schur complements. Instead of expressing the complete PDE solution as one large binary optimization problem, quadratic unconstrained binary optimization is used only to construct reusable local inverse factors. These factors are computed during an offline stage, decoded and stored, and then reused in an ordinary classical block solve for subsequent righthand sides. The optimizer facing problem size is governed by the local block size and chosen numerical precision, rather than by the dimension of the full spatial grid. We develop the mathematical formulation, analyze the accuracy and resource requirements of the binary representation, and examine the method on representative finite difference PDE problems, including execution of the local optimization stage on quantum optimization hardware. The resulting architecture provides a reusable interface between conventional numerical linear algebra and QUBO based quantum optimization.
tldr: The paper presents a hybrid offline-online framework that uses QUBO-based quantum optimization to compute reusable local block-Schur inverse factors for fixed-operator finite-difference PDE solvers.
motivation: Many PDE simulations require repeated solves of linear systems with a fixed matrix and varying right-hand sides, motivating reusable numerical components that can leverage quantum optimization without embedding the full PDE solve in a single large QUBO.
method: The discretized operator is partitioned into small coupled blocks and reduced via block Schur complements; QUBO is used only offline to construct local inverse factors, which are decoded, stored, and reused in a classical block solve.
result: The authors develop the formulation, analyze accuracy and resource requirements of the binary representation, and demonstrate the method on representative finite-difference PDE problems, including execution of the local optimization stage on quantum optimization hardware.
conclusion: The work provides a reusable interface between conventional numerical linear algebra and QUBO-based quantum optimization, but it is an applied numerical/quantum-optimization contribution rather than a result in the user's specified research directions.

title: Certified Fourier Rounding For The Real Grothendieck Inequality
authors: Bo Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a computer-assisted proof that the real Grothendieck constant is strictly smaller than [MATH]. The proof provides a complete interval-arithmetic realization of Ren's five-variable construction. A finite Fourier calculation encloses every scalar coefficient through degree [MATH]; a fourth-derivative estimate on the entire unit circle bounds the remaining coefficient sum by [MATH]. Exact rational arithmetic then certifies the final inequality. We include the transfer to all finite real matrices and arbitrary vector dimensions, the analytic quadrature errors, the rational parameters, and source code for checking and regenerating the certificate.
tldr: A computer-assisted, interval-arithmetic proof that the real Grothendieck constant is strictly below 1.7822 (or similar bound), refining Ren's five-variable construction via certified Fourier coefficient enclosures.
motivation: The exact value of the real Grothendieck constant is a long-standing open problem in functional analysis; prior five-variable constructions gave non-rigorous numerical evidence, so a fully certified proof is needed.
method: Ren's five-variable construction is realized in interval arithmetic, with a finite Fourier computation enclosing scalar coefficients up to a fixed degree, a fourth-derivative bound on the unit circle controlling the tail sum, and exact rational arithmetic certifying the final inequality.
result: A rigorous, machine-checkable certificate establishes that the real Grothendieck constant is strictly smaller than the claimed constant, with transfer to all finite real matrices and arbitrary dimensions, including quadrature error analysis and source code.
conclusion: The work converts a numerical heuristic into a certified mathematical theorem about the real Grothendieck constant, providing reproducible interval-arithmetic certificates.

title: Two-parameter Toeplitz-type Operators Between Fock Spaces
authors: Xingtang Dong, Zipeng Wang, Kehe Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study a two-parameter family of Toeplitz-type operators [MATH] on the Fock space [MATH] for [MATH] we obtain sharp conditions for [MATH] such that [MATH] is bounded or compact. In the Hilbert space case [MATH], we also study the Berezin transform of [MATH] and membership of [MATH] in Schatten classes. Furthermore, we find a class of noncompact operators whose Berezin transforms nevertheless vanish at infinity.
tldr: The authors introduce a two-parameter family of Toeplitz-type operators acting between Fock spaces and characterize their boundedness, compactness, and Schatten-class membership via Berezin transforms.
motivation: Toeplitz operators on Fock spaces are a central object in complex analysis and operator theory, but two-parameter generalizations between distinct Fock spaces had not been systematically characterized.
method: Sharp conditions on the parameters are derived for boundedness and compactness; in the Hilbert-space case the Berezin transform is computed and used to test membership in Schatten classes, with an explicit construction of noncompact operators whose Berezin transforms vanish at infinity.
result: Complete boundedness/compactness criteria are obtained, Schatten-class membership is characterized through the Berezin transform, and a counterexample class shows that vanishing Berezin transform does not imply compactness.
conclusion: The work extends Toeplitz operator theory on Fock spaces to a two-parameter setting and clarifies the limits of Berezin-transform-based compactness criteria.

title: Coactions Of Weak Multiplier Hopf Algebras
authors: Nan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we investigate the notion of a coaction for a weak multiplier Hopf algebra. We show that there is a duality for actions and coactions of weak algebraic quantum groups. Then we obtain the well known Blattner-Montgomery duality theorem for weak algebraic quantum groups in the framework of dual pairs. We form a Morita context when the weak multiplier Hopf algebra admits a two-sided faithful integral and show that the coaction is Galois if and only if the map in the Morita context is surjective. As an application, we obtain the result that a grading by any groupoid [MATH] can be considered as a [MATH]-comodule algebra. We also construct a Morita context connecting the smash product [MATH] and the coinvariant subalgebra [MATH]. Finally we construct an isomorphism between [MATH] and [MATH] when [MATH] is graded by [MATH].
tldr: A pure mathematics paper developing the theory of coactions for weak multiplier Hopf algebras, including duality theorems, Morita contexts, and Galois conditions.
motivation: Weak multiplier Hopf algebras generalize algebraic quantum groups to settings without identity, and a systematic theory of their actions and coactions—together with a Blattner–Montgomery-type duality—was still missing.
method: Algebraic/operator-algebraic techniques: dual pairs of weak multiplier Hopf algebras, two-sided faithful integrals, smash products, coinvariant subalgebras, and construction of Morita contexts to characterize Galois coactions.
result: Duality for actions and coactions is established, the Blattner–Montgomery duality theorem is recovered, and a coaction is shown to be Galois iff the associated Morita context map is surjective; groupoid gradings are recovered as comodule algebras.
conclusion: The framework unifies and extends duality and Galois theory for weak algebraic quantum groups, with groupoid gradings as an application, though it remains purely structural mathematics with no direct quantum-information or thermodynamic content.

title: A Gauge-Invariant Finite Element Method For The Time-Dependent Ginzburg--Landau Equations
authors: Huadong Gao, Yuhui Huang, Wen Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that the Ginzburg--Landau equations are gauge invariant. The most popular gauge choice in practical simulations is the temporal gauge, also known as the zero electric potential gauge. However, the commonly used N\'ed\'elec approximations may produce spurious giant vortices on domains with re-entrant corners. To address this issue while retaining the N\'ed\'elec approximation, we propose a finite element scheme that preserves the gauge invariance of the time-dependent Ginzburg--Landau equations at the discrete level. Under the temporal gauge, the method employs lowest-order N\'ed\'elec edge elements for the magnetic potential and continuous piecewise-linear elements for the order parameter on triangular and tetrahedral meshes, and yields a linear, decoupled formulation that requires only the solution of linear systems at each time step. We prove that the scheme is gauge invariant, preserves a discrete maximum bound principle for the order parameter, [MATH], and satisfies a discrete energy law under mild step-size and mesh conditions. Numerical experiments confirm these theoretical properties. In particular, on domains with re-entrant corners, the scheme computes the correct physical solution, whereas conventional temporal-gauge discretizations with N\'ed\'elec elements produce an unphysical solution.
tldr: The authors propose a gauge-invariant finite element discretization of the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equations that avoids spurious vortices produced by conventional Nédélec temporal-gauge schemes on domains with re-entrant corners.
motivation: Standard temporal-gauge Nédélec approximations of the gauge-invariant Ginzburg-Landau equations can generate unphysical giant vortices near re-entrant corners, motivating a discretization that preserves gauge invariance at the discrete level.
method: Lowest-order Nédélec edge elements are used for the magnetic potential and continuous piecewise-linear elements for the order parameter on triangular and tetrahedral meshes, yielding a linear decoupled scheme requiring only linear solves per time step.
result: The scheme is proven gauge invariant, satisfies a discrete maximum bound principle for the order parameter and a discrete energy law under mild step-size and mesh conditions, and numerical experiments confirm correct physical solutions on re-entrant-corner domains where conventional schemes fail.
conclusion: Preserving discrete gauge invariance removes spurious vortex artifacts while retaining computational efficiency, making the method suitable for practical TDGL simulations.

title: Blockchain Participation Games With Upfront Contribution Commitment
authors: Jing Chen Zhenhe Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchain participation games model costly entry, random selection, and threshold success; their retraction variants charge completion costs only to selected contributors. We study committee tasks requiring operators to reserve computing or communication capacity before assignment, so preparation costs are incurred even when capacity remains unused. Users choose abstention, bare registration without preparation, or binding commitment to contribute if selected. Success requires sufficiently many selected contributors, creates public value, and may trigger separate rewards for registration and verified contribution. We characterize all pure Nash equilibria under homogeneous selection and analyze ordering under heterogeneous selection. The results distinguish free-riding on public value from registration that earns rewards without productive commitment; more frequently selected users can choose bare registration while less frequently selected users contribute. Our main result characterizes every homogeneous minimum-outlay scheme supporting full contribution, where every user commits, as a Nash equilibrium. When positive rewards are required, these schemes form a line segment. There is always an optimum with no registration reward. It eliminates every equilibrium containing bare registrants at minimum outlay while retaining the full-contribution equilibrium; threshold-coordination failures may remain. Under heterogeneous selection, a two-user instance has a unique optimum using both rewards, cheaper than every zero-registration-reward scheme supporting full contribution. Finally, if full contribution is a positive-welfare social optimum, the homogeneous zero-registration-reward design attains price of stability one. Under arbitrary independent selection probabilities, every full-contribution Nash equilibrium is also a strong equilibrium.
tldr: A game-theoretic analysis of blockchain committee participation games where users must commit capacity upfront, characterizing Nash equilibria and optimal reward schemes.
motivation: Blockchain committee-based protocols require operators to reserve computing or communication capacity before being selected, so preparation costs are sunk even if capacity goes unused; the paper asks how reward and registration schemes should be designed to induce full contribution.
method: The authors model users choosing among abstention, bare registration, or binding commitment, and characterize all pure Nash equilibria under homogeneous selection, with ordering analysis and welfare/price-of-stability results under heterogeneous and arbitrary independent selection probabilities.
result: Every homogeneous minimum-outlay scheme supporting full contribution is a Nash equilibrium; with positive rewards these schemes form a line segment, and there is always an optimum with no registration reward that eliminates bare-registrant equilibria while retaining full contribution; under heterogeneity a two-user instance uniquely optimizes using both rewards.
conclusion: Zero-registration-reward designs achieve price of stability one when full contribution is the welfare optimum, and every full-contribution equilibrium is strong under arbitrary independent selection probabilities.

title: Query-Dependent Reading For Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
authors: Krishnakumar Balasubramanian, Siddharth Bhandari, Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores [MATH] bits about [MATH] before seeing a query [MATH], and a reader probes at most [MATH] bits to estimate [MATH]. Both vectors lie in the [MATH]-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by [MATH] times the worst-case mean-squared error over [MATH], averaged over protocol randomness. First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an [MATH]-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates [MATH] and [MATH], the normalized minimax error converges to [MATH], independent of [MATH]. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020]. Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most [MATH] as [MATH]. At fixed [MATH], this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime [MATH] and [MATH], it gives normalized error at least [MATH]. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of [MATH] in the leading constant.
tldr: The paper establishes minimax separation results for quantized inner-product estimation in the static bit-probe model, showing that query-dependent reading of the stored message can exploit extra storage whereas query-independent reading cannot.
motivation: Inner-product estimation under separate storage and reading budgets arises in sketching, similarity search, and compressed-domain inference, and it was unclear whether adaptive (query-dependent) probing of a stored sketch can beat non-adaptive full-message reading.
method: The authors work in Yao's static bit-probe model with randomized protocols and unrestricted computation, proving a matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders in the query-independent regime, and constructing a two-batch Gaussian-projection plus random-threshold protocol with a finite-dimensional lower bound for fully branching readers.
result: At fixed positive rates the normalized minimax error of query-independent readers converges to a constant independent of dimension, while the query-dependent two-batch protocol achieves vanishing error as storage grows, and in the doubly sparse regime the lower bound matches the construction up to a factor of two in the leading constant.
conclusion: Adaptivity in reading is a genuine resource for quantized inner-product estimation, yielding an unbounded advantage over query-independent schemes, with the proposed protocol optimal up to a small constant factor.

title: Encoding Hyperuniformity In Geometric Networks: Structural Signatures And Diffusion Dynamics
authors: Yongyi Wang, Eli Newby, Yang Jiao, Salvatore Torquato, R\'eka Albert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disordered hyperuniformity is a recently discovered exotic state exhibiting anomalously suppressed density fluctuations at long wavelengths, and its generalization to network systems remains an important open question. Here, we show that, across a wide range of systems, geometric networks retain substantially more long-wavelength density information from the underlying point configurations than Delaunay triangulations. Within geometric networks, hyperuniformity manifests as suppressed vertex-to-vertex fluctuations in a range of network structural observables, including closeness centrality, vertex strength, and eigenvector centrality. These measures not only distinguish hyperuniform networks from non-hyperuniform ones, but also separate near-hyperuniform configurations from hyperuniform systems with strong local disorder, solving a central challenge in network hyperuniformity. We connect these structural signatures to network dynamics by introducing a relaxation-time centrality based on diffusion and demonstrate that hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit more homogeneous relaxation behavior than non-hyperuniform geometric networks. These results reveal how the suppression of large-scale density fluctuations manifests in both network structure and diffusion dynamics.
tldr: The paper studies how hyperuniformity in underlying point configurations is encoded in geometric networks and how it affects network structural observables and diffusion-based relaxation dynamics.
motivation: Hyperuniformity is well studied for point configurations but its generalization to network systems remains an open question, motivating a structural and dynamical characterization of hyperuniform geometric networks.
method: The authors compare geometric networks with Delaunay triangulations, analyze network observables such as closeness centrality, vertex strength, and eigenvector centrality, and introduce a relaxation-time centrality based on diffusion.
result: Hyperuniform geometric networks retain more long-wavelength density information than Delaunay triangulations, show suppressed vertex-to-vertex fluctuations in several structural measures, and exhibit more homogeneous diffusion relaxation than non-hyperuniform networks.
conclusion: The work identifies structural signatures of hyperuniformity in geometric networks and connects suppressed large-scale density fluctuations to more homogeneous network diffusion dynamics.

title: Microcomb Spectral Fingerprinting Enables Parts-per-trillion Methane Detection With Low Humidity Cross-sensitivity
authors: Shiyan Cao, Yinchao Xu, Judith Su
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical frequency combs have transformed molecular spectroscopy by enabling broadband, high-resolution analysis, yet they are conventionally used as light sources to interrogate external samples. Here, we introduce an integrated microcomb sensing architecture that unifies resonantly enhanced evanescent sensing with multiwavelength molecular fingerprinting in a single ultrahigh-quality-factor silica microresonator. Gaseous analytes interact directly with the evanescent field of light recirculating within the resonator, enhancing sensitivity while encoding analyte-induced perturbations across the microcomb's collective spectral response. Rather than relying on a single optical resonance, we exploit distributed responses across multiple comb lines to generate multidimensional molecular fingerprints. Adding more comb lines systematically improves analyte discrimination, showing that the microcomb provides sensing information beyond what individual spectral channels offer. Using methane as a model analyte, we achieve an estimated detection limit of 178 parts per trillion, with minimal spectral responses to ammonia, carbon monoxide, hexane, and water vapor at relative humidities up to 90%. By replacing physically long interaction paths with resonant light recirculation in an ultrahigh-Q microresonator, this architecture brings compact optical sensing into the parts-per-trillion regime while exploiting distributed spectral information for chemical identification.
tldr: An ultrahigh-Q silica microresonator microcomb architecture performs broadband evanescent molecular fingerprinting, detecting methane at an estimated 178 parts-per-trillion with low humidity cross-sensitivity.
motivation: Optical frequency combs are typically used only as external light sources for spectroscopy; the authors aim to unify resonant evanescent sensing and multiwavelength fingerprinting within a single integrated microcomb device.
method: Gaseous analytes interact directly with the evanescent field of recirculating light in a high-Q silica microresonator, and distributed responses across multiple comb lines are combined into multidimensional molecular fingerprints rather than relying on a single resonance.
result: Using methane as a model analyte, they report an estimated detection limit of 178 ppt with minimal spectral response to ammonia, carbon monoxide, hexane, and water vapor up to 90% relative humidity; discrimination improves as more comb lines are added.
conclusion: Resonant light recirculation replaces long physical interaction paths, enabling compact parts-per-trillion chemical sensing with distributed spectral information for identification.

title: Quantum-Classical Iterative Refinement For The Pressure-Poisson Equation On Nisq Hardware
authors: Doyeol "david" Ahn (department Of Electrical And Computer Engineering, University Of Seoul, Seoul, Republic Of Korea 2 Singularity Quantum Inc., Newport Beach, CA, USA 3 Center For Quantum Information Processing, University Of Seoul, Seoul, Republic Of Korea 4 School Of Mechanical And Aerospace Engineering, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Republic Of Korea 5 National Quantum Laboratory At Maryland), Byeongyong Park, Rho Shin Myong, Franz Klein
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a hybrid quantum-classical iterative refinement for the pressure-Poisson equation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes projection method on noisy quantum hardware. Rather than solving the pressure equation once per time step, we solve it repeatedly for the normalized residual and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual. As a result, the error of the quantum solve enters as a contraction factor [MATH] of the residual rather than as an error floor. This removes the requirement of a state infidelity below [MATH] that was estimated for single-solve schemes. With a boundary-consistent staggered (MAC) discretization, the pressure residual equals the velocity divergence left after projection up to the factor [MATH]. On the IBM processor ibm_cleveland, a four-qubit ([MATH]) problem reached a relative residual below [MATH] within eight to ten corrections in all 20 runs of a pre-registered experiment, whereas a single solve with a comparable number of shots stopped at 0.33-0.59. In a six-qubit ([MATH]) pilot, all three runs reached the same tolerance in 13 corrections. On the IonQ Forte processor, a manufactured-solution benchmark reached [MATH] in nine corrections, with a pressure error of [MATH]. Finally, we carried out the variational training itself on ibm_cleveland, so that every sampled value of the cost function was obtained from hardware measurements. The residual fell to [MATH] in seven corrections, below the pre-specified tolerance of [MATH], at the rate predicted by a noise model and with 24 min of QPU time.
tldr: This paper develops a hybrid quantum-classical iterative refinement method for solving the pressure-Poisson equation on NISQ hardware, improving residual error without requiring very low state infidelity.
motivation: Solving the pressure-Poisson equation repeatedly in incompressible Navier-Stokes simulations is costly, and single quantum solves on noisy hardware suffer from error floors that limit accuracy.
method: The authors repeatedly solve for the normalized residual and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual, using a boundary-consistent staggered MAC discretization and variational quantum training on IBM and IonQ processors.
result: On ibm_cleveland, a four-qubit problem reached relative residual below the tolerance within eight to ten corrections in all 20 runs, while single-solve schemes stopped at 0.33-0.59; a six-qubit pilot and IonQ Forte benchmark also reached target tolerances.
conclusion: The iterative refinement converts quantum-solve error into a contraction factor rather than an error floor, enabling useful pressure-Poisson solves on current noisy quantum hardware.

title: Spontaneous Particle-hole Symmetry Breaking In A Disordered Two-site Quantum Breakdown Model
authors: Kinya Guan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model. The model is solvable in the limit of a large number of fermionic modes on each site. For a small ratio of the numbers of modes on the two sites, we derive the free energy analytically and find a finite-temperature symmetry-breaking transition. This transition changes from continuous to first order as the number of fermions produced in each conversion increases. Numerical results show that both types of transition persist beyond this regime, with an order-parameter exponent close to [MATH] for continuous transitions.
tldr: The paper studies spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking and finite-temperature phase transitions in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model solvable in the large-mode limit.
motivation: The work aims to understand symmetry-breaking transitions in a quantum breakdown model with disorder and many fermionic modes, including how transition order depends on fermion production.
method: The model is solved analytically in the large-number-of-modes limit, deriving the free energy for small mode-number ratios, supplemented by numerical checks beyond this regime.
result: A finite-temperature symmetry-breaking transition is found, which changes from continuous to first order as the number of fermions produced per conversion increases; numerics show both transitions persist beyond the solvable regime with an order-parameter exponent near a stated value.
conclusion: The paper characterizes spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking and transition universality in a disordered quantum breakdown model, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Charge-Selective Displacement Of Spatiotemporal Optical Vortices At A Spatially Uniform Time Boundary
authors: Peilong Yang Chao Mei
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At a spatially uniform, in-plane-isotropic time boundary, the transverse displacement of a spatiotemporal optical vortex changes sign with its topological charge, despite a charge-independent conversion weight. Radial spectral filtering couples to the vortex phase while preserving identical converted spectral intensities for opposite charges. For a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum, the displacement follows the logarithmic slope of the spectral weight and occurs with zero mean transverse momentum. In a finite pumped GaAs waveguide, unequal attenuation during extraction adds angular deflection. Independent Maxwell--Drude simulations test this extraction-induced response and give [MATH]~mrad before detector filtering. Calculated centroid traces at multiple planes separate propagation-induced drift from position offsets.
tldr: The paper studies charge-dependent transverse displacement of spatiotemporal optical vortices at a spatially uniform time boundary, including extraction-induced angular deflection in a pumped GaAs waveguide.
motivation: The work aims to understand how topological charge affects vortex displacement at temporal boundaries and how radial spectral filtering and finite-waveguide extraction modify the response.
method: The authors analyze a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum at an in-plane-isotropic time boundary and perform independent Maxwell-Drude simulations of a finite pumped GaAs waveguide with detector filtering.
result: The displacement changes sign with topological charge while conversion weights remain charge-independent, and extraction in the finite waveguide adds angular deflection of order milliradians before detector filtering.
conclusion: The results clarify charge-selective vortex displacement and extraction-induced deflection at time boundaries, with centroid traces separating propagation drift from position offsets.

title: An Accurate Zeroth-Order Perturbation Theory For Solving Power-Law Potentials Within The Framework Of The Asymptotic Iteration Method
authors: A. J. Sous, Ibsal Assi, Nasser Saad
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spherically symmetric singular potentials have a wide range of applications, such as molecular and atomic physics. In this work, we present a zeroth-order perturbation theory for solving the Schr\"odinger equation within the framework of the asymptotic iteration method (AIM). We rely on exponential and hyperbolic potential ansatz substitutions, where the difference between the original and new potential is treated as a small perturbation. Each potential ansatz has a free parameter chosen small enough to give an accurate zeroth-order perturbative wave equation solution. This method avoids the oscillatory behavior observed in the asymptotic iteration solutions when applying the AIM to such problems. Finally, we illustrate our approach by solving a few problems, particularly potentials with quartic and sextic singularities. We compare our results with those obtained via other methods and find good agreement.
tldr: The paper develops a zeroth-order perturbation method within the asymptotic iteration method to solve the Schrödinger equation for spherically symmetric singular power-law potentials.
motivation: Singular potentials are important in atomic and molecular physics, but standard asymptotic iteration methods can exhibit oscillatory or inaccurate behavior for such potentials.
method: The authors introduce exponential and hyperbolic potential ansatz substitutions, treat the difference from the original potential as a small perturbation, and choose a free parameter small enough to obtain an accurate zeroth-order wave equation solution.
result: They illustrate the approach on quartic and sextic singular potentials and find good agreement with results from other methods while avoiding oscillatory asymptotic iteration solutions.
conclusion: The proposed zeroth-order perturbation theory provides an accurate and stable way to solve power-law singular potentials within the asymptotic iteration method framework.

title: Causal Information Exchange As A Necessary Condition For Adaptive Regulation: A Perturbational Framework For Life And Agency
authors: Brian Luvalle, Abicumaran Uthamacumaran, Hector Zenil
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information exchange can support living organisation without providing a sufficient criterion for life. We develop a perturbational framework that distinguishes causal transmission, directional imbalance, internal retention, response structure and functional regulation. Randomised interventions define Shannon information channels; for deterministic binary recipients, their context-conditioned mutual information is exactly a paired perturbation-response indicator. Spatial and temporal averages of these local channels measure information-exposure density, rather than joint information or conserved information flux. Complementary Coding Theorem Method and Block Decomposition Method (BDM) estimates describe response and trajectory structure. A same-shaped zero-mask reference separates raw BDM from a structural contrast; neither is a channel mutual information. Retained exploratory BDM plots are distinguished from the normalised causal-channel results. Retention-weighted coupling and directionality obey algebraic bounds, and ensemble reciprocity need not imply reciprocity within individual contexts. For a specified binary sensor--internal-channel--actuator task, we derive a positive information lower bound from successful regulation and construct controllers with identical information profiles but opposite functional outcomes. A study of 2,000 ordered elementary-cellular-automaton rule pairs, six detailed examples, recurrence and lossless coding analyses, and a signed-network extension demonstrates dissociations among perturbational responsiveness, structural regularity and recurrence. The results establish causal information as a necessary resource for the stated form of adaptive regulation, while showing why neither causal coupling nor response complexity alone measures agency or life.
tldr: The paper proposes a perturbational information-theoretic framework to characterize causal exchange, retention, and regulation as necessary but not sufficient conditions for life and agency.
motivation: The authors aim to distinguish causal information transmission from broader notions of information exchange and to clarify why coupling or complexity alone cannot serve as sufficient criteria for adaptive regulation or life.
method: They define randomized-intervention Shannon channels, use context-conditioned mutual information, compare Coding Theorem Method and Block Decomposition Method estimates, and analyze cellular-automaton rule pairs and signed-network extensions.
result: They derive algebraic bounds on retention-weighted coupling and directionality, obtain a positive information lower bound for successful regulation in a binary sensor-internal-channel-actuator task, and construct controllers with identical information profiles but opposite functional outcomes.
conclusion: Causal information is established as a necessary resource for the specified form of adaptive regulation, while causal coupling and response complexity alone are shown to be insufficient measures of agency or life.

title: Singular Aubry--Mather Sets For A Homogeneous Single-Input Control System
authors: Cristian Mendico Bernard Bonnard
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an Aubry--Mather theory for the abnormal arcs of a time-minimal single-input affine control system in dimension three with homogeneous cubic drift. We show that the Bonnard--Kupka semi-invariant defining the abnormal locus is a Darboux polynomial of the desingularized singular field, with an explicit cofactor; this gives the invariance of the abnormal locus, a closed formula for the multiplier of its periodic components and, through the antipodal symmetry of the model, their description as lifts of ovals of a real plane quintic. For a compact invariant set of a singular flow we then define a singular Aubry--Mather structure, whose Lagrangian is supported on the graph of the singular field and whose Hamilton--Jacobi equation is linear in the momentum. We prove a duality formula for the critical value, the existence of critical subsolutions strict outside the Aubry set, and the covariance of the structure under time changes. On the abnormal locus the structure selects the periodic components of minimal average cost, governs transverse stability, and exhibits a sharp obstruction to correctors along heteroclinic cycles; for the radial exponent of the homogeneous dynamics, the corrector is the periodic part of the logarithmic radius. An explicit cubic example illustrates the results.
tldr: The paper develops an Aubry–Mather theory for abnormal arcs in a three-dimensional time-minimal single-input affine control system with homogeneous cubic drift.
motivation: It aims to characterize singular abnormal extremals and their invariant sets in a control-geometric setting, using Aubry–Mather-type variational structures.
method: The authors show that the Bonnard–Kupka semi-invariant is a Darboux polynomial of the desingularized singular field, define a singular Aubry–Mather structure, and prove duality, subsolution, covariance, and stability results.
result: They obtain explicit descriptions of periodic components via ovals of a real plane quintic, a critical-value duality formula, strict critical subsolutions outside the Aubry set, and a sharp obstruction to correctors along heteroclinic cycles.
conclusion: The work provides a geometric/variational theory for abnormal extremals in homogeneous control systems, illustrated by an explicit cubic example, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Representing Information On Dna Using Patterns Induced By Enzymatic Labeling
authors: Daniella Bar-Lev, Eitan Yaakobi, Zohar Yakhini, Tuvi Etzion
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enzymatic DNA labeling is a powerful tool with applications in biochemistry, molecular biology, biotechnology, medical science, and genomic research. This paper contributes to the evolving field of DNA-based data storage by presenting a formal framework for modeling DNA labeling in strings, specifically tailored for data storage purposes. Our approach involves a known DNA molecule as a template for labeling, employing patterns induced by a set of designed labels to represent information. One hypothetical implementation can use CRISPR-Cas9 and gRNA reagents for labeling. Various aspects of the general labeling channel, including fixed-length labels, are explored, and upper bounds on the maximum size of the corresponding codes are given. The study includes the development of an efficient encoder-decoder pair that is proven to be optimal in terms of maximum code size under specific conditions. The codewords for this framework are codesets, i.e., each codeword is a collection of a few labels. Of special interest are codes whose codesets contain fixed-length labels. Their construction and analysis are tied to de Bruijn sequences and constrained coding.
tldr: The paper proposes a formal coding framework for DNA-based data storage using enzymatic labeling patterns, including code constructions and bounds for label sets.
motivation: DNA labeling with tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 offers a way to encode information in patterns on a template DNA molecule, motivating a rigorous coding-theoretic treatment for data storage.
method: The authors model a labeling channel with fixed-length labels, derive upper bounds on maximum code sizes, and construct optimal encoder-decoder pairs under specific conditions, linking fixed-length-label codesets to de Bruijn sequences and constrained coding.
result: They characterize the labeling channel, provide bounds on code size, and develop efficient optimal codes for certain fixed-length-label scenarios.
conclusion: The work establishes a coding framework for DNA labeling-based storage but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Certifiably Correct Fr\'echet Means In Orbit Spaaces
authors: Dustin G. Mixon, Tom Needham, Nathan Willey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Fr\'echet means in orbit spaces of finite orthogonal group actions. Since computing these means is NP-hard in general, we take inspiration from group synchronization to develop tractable spectral and semidefinite relaxations. Pairwise alignment certifies global optimality and we develop a semidefinite certificate that can extend beyond this condition. For Gaussian data modulo sign, we prove that our certificate succeeds in a high-noise regime where alignment fails. Numerical experiments evaluate these methods in various settings, including summarizing ensembles of districting plans and clustering time series.
tldr: The paper develops tractable spectral and semidefinite relaxations for computing Fréchet means in orbit spaces of finite orthogonal group actions, with certifiable optimality conditions.
motivation: Fréchet means in orbit spaces are NP-hard to compute in general, motivating relaxations inspired by group synchronization and global optimality certificates.
method: The authors use pairwise alignment as a certificate and derive a semidefinite certificate that can succeed beyond alignment, with Gaussian data modulo sign as a case study.
result: They prove the certificate succeeds in a high-noise regime where alignment fails and evaluate the methods numerically on districting plans and time-series clustering.
conclusion: The work provides certifiably correct relaxations for orbit-space Fréchet means, with guarantees extending beyond pairwise-alignment regimes.

title: Analysis And Approximation For Inverse Potential Problem Of Space-dependent Variable-exponent Sub-diffusion In Heterogeneous Medium
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Chunlong Sun, Xiangcheng Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomalous transport in complex heterogeneous medium is often characterized by non-Markovian memory effects and spatially varying trapping properties. From the point of view of continuous-time random walks, such heterogeneity can be described by a position-dependent heavy-tailed waiting-time density [MATH], where [MATH] is the local anomalous exponent. This microscopic interpretation naturally leads to the sub-diffusion with a space-dependent variable exponent [MATH]. Compared with constant-exponent models, the variable-exponent fractional operators generally do not commute with the spatial Laplacian, which makes both the forward and inverse analysis substantially more delicate. This paper investigates the inverse problem of recovering a spatially dependent radiative or potential coefficient in variable-exponent sub-diffusion from terminal observation data. We formulate the inverse problem as a nonlinear fixed-point equation and prove that the associated fixed-point operator is monotone such that the fixed-point iteration converges decreasingly to the unique solution. We further establish a Lipschitz-type conditional stability estimate for the terminal observation map, which also implies uniqueness of the inverse problem for sufficiently large terminal time. For numerical reconstruction, we develop a fully discrete finite element scheme and derive an error estimate for the inverse problem. Numerical simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the method, even in the presence of noisy data.
tldr: The paper studies an inverse coefficient problem for space-dependent variable-exponent sub-diffusion equations in heterogeneous media, proving monotone fixed-point convergence, conditional stability, and finite-element error estimates with numerical validation.
motivation: Anomalous transport in heterogeneous media exhibits non-Markovian memory and spatially varying trapping, motivating variable-exponent fractional sub-diffusion models whose operators do not commute with the Laplacian, complicating forward and inverse analysis.
method: The inverse problem of recovering a spatially dependent radiative/potential coefficient from terminal data is cast as a nonlinear fixed-point equation; monotonicity of the fixed-point operator is proved and a fully discrete finite element scheme is developed with error estimates.
result: The fixed-point iteration converges decreasingly to a unique solution, a Lipschitz-type conditional stability estimate for the terminal observation map yields uniqueness for sufficiently large terminal time, and numerical simulations confirm effectiveness including with noisy data.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analysis and a convergent numerical scheme for inverse variable-exponent sub-diffusion problems, extending classical constant-exponent fractional inverse theory.

title: Commutative Exact Superalgebras And Super-modular Tensor Categories
authors: A. Zuevsky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the theory of commutative exact algebras in braided finite tensor categories (Shimizu-Yadav) to superalgebras, motivated by extensions of vertex operator (super)algebras. For a braided category [MATH] let [MATH] be the category of [MATH]-graded objects with the Koszul-signed braiding. It is the underlying category of the supercategory of Creutzig-Kanade-McRae. A supercommutative superalgebra [MATH] in [MATH] is the same as a commutative algebra [MATH] in [MATH], and super-local modules are the local [MATH]-modules. Hence rigidity, pivotality and ribbon statements are instances of the ordinary theorems, with the ribbon condition [MATH], [MATH], where [MATH] is fixed by the statistics of the odd part. For [MATH] non-degenerate and [MATH] haploid and exact we prove that the category of super-local modules is a braided finite tensor category whose M\"uger center is [MATH]. It is the centralizer of a fermion in a non-degenerate category obtained by condensing in [MATH]. If [MATH] is ribbon and [MATH] is symmetric Frobenius it is ribbon. We construct examples from graded simple currents, treat the free fermion and the symplectic fermion, and compare with Creutzig-Kanade-McRae and Creutzig-McRae-Shimizu-Yadav.
tldr: This paper extends commutative exact algebra theory in braided finite tensor categories to superalgebras and studies the resulting super-local module categories.
motivation: The work is motivated by extensions of vertex operator superalgebras and by developing a superalgebraic analogue of Shimizu-Yadav's commutative exact algebras in braided tensor categories.
method: It uses Koszul-signed braiding on graded objects, relates supercommutative superalgebras to ordinary commutative algebras, and analyzes rigidity, pivotality, ribbon structure, and Muger centers for super-local modules.
result: For non-degenerate haploid exact supercommutative superalgebras, the category of super-local modules is a braided finite tensor category whose Muger center is the centralizer of a fermion; ribbon and Frobenius conditions are also characterized.
conclusion: The framework unifies and extends several constructions in super-modular tensor categories, with examples from graded simple currents, free fermions, and symplectic fermions.

title: Optimal Degree Bounds For Sum-of-squares Representations
authors: Alexander Taveira Blomenhofer, Sander Gribling, Didier Henrion, Milan Korda, Poornendu Kumar, Victor Magron, Lucas Slot, Luis Felipe Vargas, Juan Vera
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The moment-sum-of-squares (SOS) hierarchy provides a sequence of bounds on the minimum of a polynomial over a basic closed semialgebraic set, i.e., a subset of [MATH] defined by finitely many polynomial constraints. We establish optimal bounds on the error of the SOS hierarchy in the following settings: 1. If the constraints define an Archimedean quadratic module: the error of the Putinar-based hierarchy at level [MATH] is [MATH] in the worst case. 2. If the constraints define a compact semialgebraic set: the error of the Schm\"udgen-based hierarchy at level [MATH] is [MATH] in the worst case. 3. If the constraints define an Archimedean quadratic module and satisfy linear independence constraint qualification conditions (LICQ): the error of the hierarchy at level [MATH] is [MATH] in the worst case. Here, the upper bound holds already for the Putinar-based hierarchy, while the lower bound holds even against the Schm\"udgen-based hierarchy. Equivalently, these give best-possible effective versions of Putinar's and Schm\"udgen's Positivstellens\"atze for these settings (in terms of their dependence on [MATH]).
tldr: The paper establishes optimal worst-case degree bounds on the error of the moment-sum-of-squares hierarchy for polynomial optimization over semialgebraic sets, giving best-possible effective versions of Putinar's and Schmüdgen's Positivstellensätze.
motivation: The SOS hierarchy's convergence rate and the degree dependence of Positivstellensatz representations were known only up to non-optimal bounds; sharp, setting-by-setting error bounds were missing.
method: Constructs explicit worst-case polynomial instances and combines algebraic degree estimates for Putinar- and Schmüdgen-type representations, including settings with Archimedean quadratic modules and LICQ conditions, to match upper and lower bounds.
