result: Optimal error bounds are proven at level d for Archimedean quadratic modules, compact semialgebraic sets, and LICQ-regular settings, with upper bounds holding for the Putinar hierarchy and lower bounds even against the Schmüdgen hierarchy.
conclusion: The results settle the sharp degree dependence of the SOS hierarchy and yield best-possible effective Positivstellensätze, with implications for the complexity of polynomial optimization algorithms.

title: Convergence Of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models: A R\'{e}nyi Divergence Perspective
authors: Wenliang Liu, Santiago Mazuelas, Guanding Yu, Renjie Liao, Lele Wang, Yuan Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for generative modeling by transforming standard Gaussian inputs into outputs that approximate a target distribution. While DDPMs have been proved to converge in total variation, KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance, these discrepancy measures share a fundamental limitation of being insensitive to distributional mismatch in low-probability regions. To address this, we adopt the stronger R\'enyi divergence as the discrepancy measure. Leveraging a Girsanov-type change-of-measure argument, we establish the first R\'enyi characterization of DDPMs to the best of our knowledge, showing that the total error decomposes into a mixing error, a discretization error, and a score estimation error. We assume the target distribution is sub-Gaussian and characterize the score error via the cumulant generating function, relaxing both the log-Sobolev-inequality and [MATH]-score-error conditions used in prior R\'enyi divergence analyses of inexact Langevin Monte Carlo, a score-based sampling algorithm closely related to DDPM. Our results also establish an iteration complexity for achieving [MATH]-accuracy in [MATH]-R\'enyi divergence that is asymptotically proportional to [MATH]. Finally, by extending our analysis, we establish the first R\'enyi divergence convergence guarantee for critically damped DDPMs, a kinetic variant governed by critically damped Langevin dynamics. Similar to existing characterizations of critically damped DDPMs, this result shares the structural scaling of standard DDPMs, differing by at most a logarithmic factor in the mixing error exponent, and supports the conjecture that critically damped DDPMs do not yield a theoretical improvement.
tldr: The paper establishes the first Rényi-divergence convergence characterization for denoising diffusion probabilistic models, decomposing the total error into mixing, discretization, and score-estimation components.
motivation: Existing convergence guarantees for DDPMs use total variation, KL divergence, or Wasserstein distance, which are insensitive to distributional mismatch in low-probability regions; Rényi divergence provides a stronger discrepancy measure.
method: A Girsanov-type change-of-measure argument is combined with a sub-Gaussian target assumption and a cumulant-generating-function characterization of the score error, relaxing prior log-Sobolev and score-error conditions used in Rényi analyses of Langevin Monte Carlo.
result: The analysis yields an iteration complexity for achieving Rényi accuracy asymptotically proportional to the target precision, and extends to critically damped DDPMs, showing the same structural scaling up to a logarithmic factor in the mixing error exponent.
conclusion: The work provides tighter convergence theory for diffusion generative models and supports the conjecture that critically damped DDPMs offer no theoretical improvement over standard DDPMs.

title: When Are Monomial Symmetric Polynomials Hard?
authors: Markus Bl\"aser, Radu Curticapean, Sagnik Dutta, Gorav Jindal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a partition [MATH] and [MATH], the monomial symmetric polynomial is defined as $[MATH][MATH][MATH]m_{}$: If a family of partitions contains polynomially many distinct parts, then the corresponding monomial symmetric polynomials (on sufficiently many variables) are VNP-complete. If the number of distinct parts is constant, the family admits polynomial-size circuits. Thus the only remaining gap concerns the intermediate regime where the number of distinct parts grows subpolynomially. As part of our proof, we use combinatorial properties of matching polynomials to establish VNP-hardness of the perfect matching polynomial for blow-up graphs; these are graphs with non-generic edge-weights that are obtained by "blowing up" a smaller graph. We reduce these matching polynomials to monomial-symmetric polynomials by combining classical techniques from algebraic complexity theory with structural properties of Sidon sets.
tldr: The paper characterizes when families of monomial symmetric polynomials are VNP-complete versus admitting polynomial-size circuits, leaving only the subpolynomial-distinct-parts regime open.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of evaluating symmetric polynomials is a natural question in algebraic complexity theory, and the hardness landscape for monomial symmetric polynomials was previously unresolved outside limiting regimes.
method: The authors establish VNP-hardness of the perfect matching polynomial on blow-up graphs using combinatorial properties of matching polynomials, then reduce these to monomial symmetric polynomials by combining classical algebraic complexity techniques with structural properties of Sidon sets.
result: Families of partitions with polynomially many distinct parts yield VNP-complete monomial symmetric polynomials (on sufficiently many variables), while constant numbers of distinct parts admit polynomial-size circuits.
conclusion: The classification nearly closes the complexity dichotomy for monomial symmetric polynomials, with only the subpolynomial-but-growing regime of distinct parts remaining as an open gap.

title: Strategic Origins Of Network Structure
authors: Rory Smead Christoph Riedl
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to [MATH] topological classes for [MATH]-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.
tldr: The paper introduces a game-graph equilibrium for payoff-driven partner-choice dynamics, showing that two-type games admit exactly four stable network topologies (assortative, disassortative, and two core-periphery forms), generalizing to higher-type interactions.
motivation: Statistical characterization of complex networks has advanced greatly, but a general mechanistic explanation for why specific mesoscale structures (e.g. core-periphery) emerge is still missing.
method: The authors define a game-graph equilibrium as the rest point of a strategic partner-choice dynamic, prove an exhaustive classification of stable topologies for two-type and M-type games, and develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to a low-dimensional game-theoretic manifold.
result: Four Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies whose payoffs distinguish cooperative from exploitative dynamics; applied to real networks such as international trade, the model gives interpretable parameters, separates states indistinguishable to conventional methods, and predicts unseen topologies without retraining.
conclusion: Network mesoscale structure can be understood as the fossilized record of strategic interaction, yielding a precise mechanistic definition of communities as strategic equivalence.

title: Explicit Criteria For Finite-Time Identification In Sparse Primal--Dual Dynamics
authors: Hassan Saoud
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when selected coordinates become and remain zero in a finite-dimensional sparse-regression primal--dual flow and its exact full resolvent iteration. Invariant balls centered at \((0,z)\), with \(z\) strictly dual feasible, give computable deadlines without rank assumptions or optimizer knowledge. The certificates may be available at initialization. We determine the smallest invariant radius for the continuous flow within this family. For a prescribed positive feasibility margin, center selection is convex and admits an exact finite conic formulation. We bound the coordinate margins for all centers in this family and give a normalized correlated example attaining the bound. A composite Bregman Lyapunov estimate proves rank-free convergence without primal uniqueness and finite identification under strict dual margins. Under restricted injectivity, the discrete gap-based deadlines multiplied by the step size tend to the continuous bound for fixed data, observed state, and certificate parameters. Numerical experiments assess certificate timing. A noisy weak-form oscillator regression illustrates the difference between fitted and physical support.
tldr: The paper derives explicit finite-time support-identification criteria for sparse primal-dual regression dynamics using invariant balls and Bregman Lyapunov estimates.
motivation: It aims to determine when coordinates of a sparse-regression primal-dual flow become and remain exactly zero, providing computable deadlines without rank assumptions or knowledge of the optimizer.
method: The analysis constructs invariant balls centered at a strictly dual-feasible point, determines the smallest invariant radius for the continuous flow, and uses a composite Bregman Lyapunov estimate to prove rank-free convergence and finite identification.
result: The paper obtains finite-time identification guarantees under strict dual margins, bounds coordinate margins over the family of centers, and shows that discrete gap-based deadlines converge to the continuous bound under restricted injectivity.
conclusion: The proposed certificates give practical finite-time support-identification criteria for sparse primal-dual dynamics, illustrated by numerical experiments including a noisy weak-form oscillator regression example.

title: Complex Representatives, Similarity Invariants, And Iterates In $\bf{U(1,1;\mathbb{H})}$
authors: Bingzhe Hou, Cailing Yao, Jiaxing He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the similarity classes of matrices in [MATH] and the iterates of their associated quaternionic M\"obius transformations. Building on the known elliptic case, we show that every parabolic or loxodromic element of [MATH] is similar, via a matrix in [MATH], to a complex matrix. Explicit complex representatives and matrices realizing these similarities are constructed for the different types. We then introduce the invariants [MATH], and prove that they form a complete system of similarity invariants for matrices in [MATH]. Finally, using the complex representation of quaternionic matrices and Chebyshev polynomials, we derive a fourth-order recurrence for a real sequence [MATH] satisfying [MATH]. Together with recurrence relations for the relevant matrix entries, this identity yields a complete classification of the quaternionic M\"obius transformation associated with [MATH], including the degenerate cases in which [MATH].
tldr: The paper classifies similarity classes of matrices in U(1,1;H) via explicit complex representatives and a complete set of invariants, and classifies the associated quaternionic Möbius transformations using Chebyshev-polynomial recurrences.
motivation: The elliptic case of quaternionic Möbius transformations was already understood, but parabolic and loxodromic elements and their similarity structure in U(1,1;H) lacked a uniform treatment with explicit constructions and complete invariants.
method: Constructive linear algebra over the quaternions: build complex matrices in U(1,1;H) that realize the similarity for each type, introduce candidate invariants and prove completeness, then use complex representations and Chebyshev polynomials to derive a fourth-order recurrence for a related real sequence.
result: Every parabolic or loxodromic element is shown to be similar to an explicit complex matrix, the proposed invariants form a complete similarity invariant system, and the recurrence yields a full classification of the associated quaternionic Möbius transformations including degenerate cases.
conclusion: The work provides a self-contained classification toolkit for U(1,1;H) matrices and their Möbius actions, extending known elliptic results to all types.

title: Unstable Entropy For Anosov Diffeomorphisms On Tori Isotopic To Anosov Linear Maps
authors: Tristan Humbert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an Anosov diffeomorphism on the [MATH]-torus which is strongly partially hyperbolic with expanding center. If [MATH] or if [MATH] is isotopic to its linear part, where the isotopy is contained in the set of partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms, we construct systems of strong-unstable and center-stable Margulis measures which are holonomy invariant. As a consequence, we obtain a characterization of measures of maximal unstable entropy in terms of their conditional measures along strong-unstable leaves. Moreover, we show that the unstable topological entropy, a measure of maximal unstable entropy and the Margulis system can be retrieved from the Pollicott-Ruelle spectrum of [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies unstable entropy and Margulis measures for Anosov diffeomorphisms on tori isotopic to linear Anosov maps.
motivation: The work aims to characterize measures of maximal unstable entropy and connect them to the Pollicott-Ruelle spectrum for partially hyperbolic Anosov systems.
method: The author constructs holonomy-invariant strong-unstable and center-stable Margulis measure systems under isotopy assumptions and analyzes their conditional measures along unstable leaves.
result: Measures of maximal unstable entropy are characterized by their conditional measures, and the unstable topological entropy, a maximal measure, and the Margulis system are recovered from the Pollicott-Ruelle spectrum.
conclusion: The results extend the thermodynamic formalism of Anosov diffeomorphisms and provide spectral interpretations of unstable entropy, but they are purely dynamical-systems results.

title: Physical Measures For Partially Hyperbolic Systems With $u$-definite Subbundles
authors: Zeya Mi Yongluo Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study \(C^{1+\alpha}\) diffeomorphisms of a compact Riemannian manifold \(\) with an attracting set \(\Lambda\) admitting a partially hyperbolic splitting \[ T_\Lambda = E^u\oplus C_1\oplus\cdots\oplus C_k\oplus E^s. \] We assume that, for every ergodic Gibbs \(u\)-state supported on \(\Lambda\), the Lyapunov exponents along each \(C_i\) are either all positive or all negative. We prove that \(\Lambda\) supports finitely many ergodic hyperbolic SRB measures whose basins cover Lebesgue almost every point of its topological basin. Our approach relies on an empirical basin-covering theorem for attracting sets with dominated splittings. Its proof hinges on a new notion of sliding suffix times, which allows us to synchronize expansion and contraction along a common empirical subsequence.
tldr: The paper proves existence and finiteness of ergodic hyperbolic SRB measures for partially hyperbolic attracting sets with u-definite subbundles, via a basin-covering theorem and sliding suffix times.
motivation: The authors study which physical measures describe the long-time statistics of partially hyperbolic systems under Lyapunov exponent sign assumptions on central subbundles.
method: They use ergodic Gibbs u-states, dominated splittings, an empirical basin-covering theorem, and introduce sliding suffix times to synchronize expansion and contraction along empirical subsequences.
result: Under the u-definite condition, the attracting set supports finitely many ergodic hyperbolic SRB measures whose basins cover Lebesgue almost every point of the topological basin.
conclusion: The work establishes a dynamical-systems result on physical measures and basin covering, outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Cooperation Without Shared Rewards Via Reciprocal Q-Augmentation
authors: Francesco Morri, Adel Abusitta, Quentin Cappart, Margarida Carvalho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and . Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
tldr: The paper proposes Reciprocal Q-Augmentation (RQA), a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to let agents learn cooperative and defective policies from only their own Q-function, inducing cooperation in social dilemmas without shared rewards.
motivation: In general-sum games, achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, but assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is unrealistic and implicitly injects cooperation into the setting.
method: RQA augments each agent's Q-function with estimates of how its actions affect other agents, derived from a latent-variable opponent model, allowing both cooperative and defecting policies to be learned from local observations alone.
result: On Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Traveler's Dilemma, and Stag Hunt, RQA agents cooperate faster and reach higher welfare than fully cooperative shared-reward algorithms, and a single RQA agent switching policies can induce cooperation in standard RL agents.
conclusion: Reciprocal Q-Augmentation enables welfare-improving cooperation in general-sum multi-agent settings without reward sharing or access to opponents' internals.

title: Local Quadratic Convergence Of Iterated Correlation Matrices: Bounds And Counterexamples
authors: Ishrak Alhajj Hassan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kruskal's unpublished manuscript on CONCOR gives a local argument for convergence of successive correlations to a prescribed two-class sign pattern. We identify a failure in its stated one-step estimate and establish a replacement bound for correlation matrices in arbitrary dimension. A geometric estimate for sign-aligned centered rows yields an explicit sufficient neighbourhood of convergence and a quadratic error bound. We construct invariant families of correlation matrices with an exact scalar recurrence in every dimension at least three. These families yield counterexamples to the original estimate in every dimension at least four. The failure persists on relatively open sets of positive-definite correlation matrices. In dimensions divisible by four, an explicitly solvable subfamily provides counterexamples arbitrarily close to the prescribed fixed point and attains the asymptotic coefficient in the new bound. Quadratic order is attained by the constructed families in every dimension at least three. These counterexamples concern the quantitative estimate, not the convergence conclusion: all the exhibited trajectories converge to their prescribed sign patterns.
tldr: This paper analyzes convergence of iterated correlation matrices related to Kruskal's CONCOR method, proving local quadratic bounds and constructing counterexamples to a prior one-step estimate.
motivation: Kruskal's unpublished CONCOR manuscript claimed a one-step convergence estimate for successive correlations to a two-class sign pattern, but the stated estimate contains a failure that needs correction.
method: The author derives a replacement bound for correlation matrices in arbitrary dimension using a geometric estimate for sign-aligned centered rows, and constructs invariant families with exact scalar recurrences.
result: The new bound gives an explicit sufficient neighborhood for convergence and a quadratic error bound, while constructed families provide counterexamples to the original estimate in dimensions at least four and attain quadratic order.
conclusion: The counterexamples invalidate the quantitative one-step estimate but not the convergence conclusion; all exhibited trajectories still converge to their prescribed sign patterns.

title: Freeform Gradient-index Media Reconstruction
authors: V. Ch\'{a}vez-Islas, F. H. Maldonado-Villamizar, E. Esp\'{i}ndola-Ramos, S. Ch\'{a}vez-Cerda, J. E. G\'{o}mez-Correa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing a gradient-index (GRIN) medium consists of determining a spatial refractive index distribution that produces a prescribed ray trajectory, an inverse problem in geometrical optics. Previous approaches have used geometrical symmetries and conserved ray quantities to address this inverse problem. Extending reconstruction to freeform media requires approaches that do not rely on these symmetries. Here, we present a three-dimensional point-wise method for reconstructing freeform GRIN media through the inverse application of local refraction. The method does not require geometrical symmetry, paraxial approximations, or prior knowledge of the iso-indicial surfaces, and is straightforward to implement. Reconstruction using two interface geometries demonstrates that different refractive index distributions can be obtained from the same prescribed trajectory function. The choice of interfaces thus provides an additional degree of freedom for optical design, subject to local refraction conditions and compatibility between overlapping reconstructed regions.
tldr: The paper presents a point-wise inverse method for reconstructing freeform gradient-index optical media from prescribed ray trajectories without requiring geometrical symmetries or paraxial approximations.
motivation: Reconstructing gradient-index media is an inverse problem in geometrical optics, and extending existing symmetry-based methods to freeform media requires symmetry-independent approaches.
method: The authors develop a three-dimensional point-wise reconstruction technique based on the inverse application of local refraction, using two interface geometries to demonstrate the method.
result: They show that different refractive-index distributions can produce the same prescribed ray trajectory, so the choice of interface geometry provides an additional design degree of freedom subject to local refraction and compatibility conditions.
conclusion: The method enables freeform GRIN medium reconstruction without prior symmetry assumptions, with potential applications in optical design.

title: Geometric Stability Of Dynamical Systems With Self-Generated State-Space Memory
authors: Robert Vrabel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a geometric stability framework for dynamical systems coupled to memory fields generated by their own state trajectories. Temporal age and state-space displacement enter a nonlinear hereditary force admitting an exact, trajectory-dependent velocity representation. A common velocity-history phase space contains both resting and uniformly translating solutions. We establish global velocity arrest under a uniform geometric memory-gain bound and obtain exact translating-speed balance laws from the full radial imprint. The response slope yields a positive longitudinal exponent on rising-speed branches, while a complementary contraction criterion gives local exponential attraction to selected descending branches in the scalar velocity dynamics, in fading-memory topology. Our principal result is a constructive geometric non-identifiability theorem: two systems with identical nonlinear force operators on an open neighborhood of rest can exhibit sharply different complete-motion behavior at the same subcritical gain. In the first, every admissible trajectory with bounded velocity prehistory comes to rest exponentially; in the second, locally attracting rest coexists with a locally attracting translating branch and an additional spectrally unstable translating branch. The infinite-memory case exhibits exponentially flat force differences, with all finite-order equilibrium derivatives agreeing despite the possibility of distinct global translating families. The framework also yields classical Volterra kernels and distributed-derivative transfer functions by linearization.
tldr: The paper develops a geometric stability framework for classical dynamical systems whose motion generates its own hereditary memory field, proving non-identifiability of the underlying force operator from complete-motion behavior.
motivation: Systems with self-generated state-space memory (age- and displacement-dependent hereditary forces) lack a general stability theory, and the authors ask whether identical force laws near rest can nonetheless produce qualitatively different long-time motion.
method: The force law is recast exactly as a trajectory-dependent velocity functional, yielding a velocity-history phase space; global velocity arrest, translating-speed balance laws, and local exponential attraction/contraction criteria are derived under a uniform geometric memory-gain bound, with fading versus infinite memory treated separately.
result: A constructive non-identifiability theorem shows two systems agreeing on the nonlinear force operator in a neighborhood of rest can differ sharply at the same subcritical gain: one arrests exponentially, the other supports coexisting attracting rest, an attracting translating branch, and an unstable translating branch; infinite memory gives exponentially flat force differences with matching finite-order equilibrium derivatives.
conclusion: Stability and asymptotic motion in self-immune memory systems are not determined by local force data, and the framework recovers classical Volterra kernels and distributed-derivative transfer functions upon linearization.

title: On Condensations Of $C_p(X)$ Spaces Onto Banach Spaces With The Weak Topology
authors: Witold Marciszewski Miko\l Aj Krupski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that for a broad class of spaces [MATH], the space [MATH] of continuous real-valued functions on [MATH] equipped with the pointwise topology maps bijectively onto any separable infinite-dimensional Banach space with the weak topology. We prove that the inverse [MATH] of any continuous bijection [MATH], where [MATH] is an arbitrary infinite Tychonoff space and [MATH] is an arbitrary normed space with the weak topology, is everywhere discontinuous. This generalizes a recent result of Kania--Kkol and solves a problem raised by Kkol, Leiderman and Michalak by providing a complete classification of function spaces [MATH] that are homeomorphic to Banach spaces with the weak topology.
tldr: The paper classifies function spaces Cp(X) that are homeomorphic to separable infinite-dimensional Banach spaces equipped with the weak topology.
motivation: It addresses a problem in infinite-dimensional topology and functional analysis concerning when spaces of continuous real-valued functions with pointwise topology can be mapped bijectively onto Banach spaces with weak topology.
method: The authors prove general results about continuous bijections from Cp(X) onto normed spaces with weak topology, showing inverse discontinuity, and use these to classify a broad class of Cp(X) spaces.
result: For a broad class of spaces X, Cp(X) maps bijectively onto any separable infinite-dimensional Banach space with weak topology; moreover, the inverse of any continuous bijection from an arbitrary infinite Tychonoff space onto a normed space with weak topology is everywhere discontinuous.
conclusion: This generalizes prior work of Kania-Kkol and solves a problem of Kkol, Leiderman, and Michalak by providing a complete classification of function spaces Cp(X) homeomorphic to Banach spaces with the weak topology.

title: Certified Neural Approximations For Parabolic Obstacle Problems
authors: Davood Damircheli
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual-trained neural surrogates carry no error guarantee, a limitation for free-boundary problems such as phase change and contact. We derive guaranteed error bounds for neural approximations of parabolic obstacle problems in first-order state--flux--multiplier form. The main result bounds the flux error of the network and the energy error of its feasible projection [MATH] by the constitutive residual, the initial mismatch, the complementarity defect, and the PDE residual weighted by [MATH], without the coercivity and norm-equivalence constants of the first-order formulation. It extends the Apushkinskaya--Repin majorant for the heat operator to general coefficients, free multipliers and a flux bound. A penetration-consistency result shows that neural triples with arbitrarily small bound exist. Outward-rounded cellwise Taylor-model enclosures turn the bound into a finite computation valid on any adaptive partition. The flux and gradient errors of the projected output are certified below [MATH] and [MATH] of the solution scale for a one-dimensional Stefan problem and, after adaptive refinement, below one half for all three trained networks on a two-dimensional expanding disk. On an expanding ellipse the gradient bound stays above one half; substitution diagnostics trace the floor of the trained networks to the projected state near the free boundary, and the remaining gap to enclosure overhead. Without a closed-form solution, a validated lower bound replaces the solution norm; there the enclosure is nearly exact, but the trained networks have errors above the solution scale and no useful accuracy is certified. The bounds control a state--flux norm, not the multiplier or the free-boundary location.
tldr: The paper derives guaranteed a posteriori error bounds for neural-network approximations of parabolic obstacle (free-boundary) problems, turning residual-based majorants into certified finite computations via outward-rounded Taylor-model enclosures.
motivation: Residual-trained neural surrogates for free-boundary problems such as phase change and contact come with no error guarantees, which is unacceptable when reliability is required.
method: The problem is cast in first-order state-flux-multiplier form, extending the Apushkinskaya-Repin majorant for the heat operator to general coefficients, free multipliers and a flux bound; cellwise Taylor-model enclosures make the bound computable on adaptive partitions.
result: Certified flux and gradient errors fall below a few percent of the solution scale for a 1D Stefan problem and below one half after adaptive refinement for three networks on a 2D expanding disk, while an expanding ellipse and a no-closed-form case yield no useful certified accuracy.
conclusion: The bounds control a state-flux norm only, not the multiplier or free-boundary location, and diagnostics attribute remaining gaps to projected-state error near the free boundary and enclosure overhead.

title: Pilot-Projected Nonlinear Self-Interference Estimation With Simultaneous Uplink Training
authors: Thomas Eriksson Seyed Mohammad Azimi-Abarghouyi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers nonlinear digital self-interference (SI) cancellation and uplink-channel estimation for single-antenna in-band full-duplex radios when a desired uplink pilot is present during SI training. In this setting, a rich nonlinear SI dictionary can absorb part of the structured pilot response, while its large and correlated set of basis functions can make reliable SI estimation difficult, particularly with limited training. During SI-coefficient estimation, we treat the unknown uplink channel as a nuisance parameter and eliminate it to obtain an equivalent reduced SI estimation problem on the orthogonal complement of the pilot convolution subspace. Since the projected nonlinear dictionary can remain ill conditioned, we develop two complementary full-dictionary estimators: a pilot-projected ridge estimator with Bayesian-information-criterion tuning (PP-RidgeBIC), which uses global ridge shrinkage, and a pilot-projected group-sparse Bayesian estimator (PP-GSBE), which learns branch-dependent Bayesian shrinkage from the data. These estimators offer two complementary operating points: PP-RidgeBIC favors computational efficiency, whereas PP-GSBE provides greater adaptivity to heterogeneous nonlinear SI components. Simulations show substantial gains in SI cancellation and uplink reception over non-projected and hard-selection alternatives; notably, PP-GSBE suppresses the residual SI below the noise floor with moderate training and consistently provides the strongest performance under nonlinear model mismatch.
tldr: The paper develops pilot-projected nonlinear self-interference estimation techniques for single-antenna in-band full-duplex radios that perform simultaneous uplink training and SI cancellation.
motivation: In full-duplex radios, a rich nonlinear SI dictionary can absorb part of the structured uplink pilot response, and its large, correlated basis makes reliable SI estimation hard under limited training.
method: The unknown uplink channel is treated as a nuisance parameter and eliminated by projecting onto the orthogonal complement of the pilot convolution subspace, yielding two full-dictionary estimators: a pilot-projected ridge estimator with BIC tuning (PP-RidgeBIC) and a pilot-projected group-sparse Bayesian estimator (PP-GSBE).
result: Simulations show substantial gains in SI cancellation and uplink reception over non-projected and hard-selection alternatives, with PP-GSBE suppressing residual SI below the noise floor under moderate training and model mismatch.
conclusion: Projecting out the pilot subspace and applying complementary shrinkage estimators provides an effective, robust approach to nonlinear SI cancellation in full-duplex systems.

title: Global Stability Of Michaelis-Menten Networks
authors: Eduardo D. Sontag
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a very nice paper, Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied networks of species coupled through Michaelis-Menten interactions. Under standard assumptions of strong connectedness and non-degeneracy, they show that there is a unique equilibrium, which is (locally) asymptotically stable. This note shows that global stability, which was stated there as an open problem, holds as well. In fact, whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition, with no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypothesis at all; those assumptions are needed only in order to guarantee existence and to cover solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant. The key is to note that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric.
tldr: This note proves that Michaelis-Menten reaction networks with a positive equilibrium are globally stable, resolving an open problem from Blanchini et al. by showing the dynamics are contractive in the Thompson part metric.
motivation: Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi established uniqueness and local asymptotic stability of equilibria in strongly connected, non-degenerate Michaelis-Menten networks, but left global stability open; this work closes that gap.
method: The author shows the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric on the positive orthant, which yields convergence of all solutions with positive initial data without connectedness or non-degeneracy assumptions.
result: Whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution starting from a positive initial condition; the earlier hypotheses are needed only for existence and for boundary trajectories.
conclusion: Global stability of Michaelis-Menten networks holds far more generally than previously shown, following from metric contraction arguments rather than network-structure conditions.

title: Zero-trace Index Of Matrices
authors: Eloise P. Misa Kennett L. Dela Rosa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The zero-trace index [MATH] of a square complex matrix [MATH] is introduced. It is defined as the largest integer [MATH] such that [MATH] admits a [MATH] compression with trace zero. This concept is analogous to the zero-dilation index [MATH] and is closely related to the [MATH]-numerical range. The [MATH]-numerical range is characterized as an intersection of half-planes, which is used to derive a formula for [MATH] that reduces its computation to the Hermitian case. Conditions for [MATH] are also established, and matrices satisfying [MATH] are characterized. Finally, the zero-trace index is determined for several classes of matrices.
tldr: The paper introduces the zero-trace index of a square complex matrix as the largest integer k for which the matrix admits a k-dimensional compression with trace zero.
motivation: The concept is motivated as an analogue of the zero-dilation index and is connected to the k-numerical range, aiming to characterize matrices through trace-zero compressions.
method: The authors characterize the k-numerical range as an intersection of half-planes and use this to derive a formula reducing the zero-trace index computation to the Hermitian case.
result: Conditions for the zero-trace index are established, matrices satisfying certain index values are characterized, and the index is determined for several matrix classes.
conclusion: The work develops a linear-algebraic invariant related to numerical ranges and compression properties, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Extension Of Surjective Isometries Between Unit Spheres Of $\ell^p$-direct Sums
authors: Min-Ruei Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study surjective isometries between the unit spheres of Banach spaces of the form [MATH], where [MATH] is nonzero and strictly convex, [MATH], and every unit vector of [MATH] has at least two distinct unit vectors at distance [MATH]. For two direct sums [MATH], [MATH], satisfying these hypotheses, we prove that every surjective isometry $[MATH][MATH]p_i[MATH][MATH][MATH]p:=p_1=p_2[MATH]L^1$-norm of the derivative. We also discuss Lipschitz and differentiable function spaces, distinguishing the consequences of our theorem from those already covered by existing extension results. Endpoint conclusions are derived separately, including the Mazur-Ulam property for the real absolutely continuous space with the sum norm.
tldr: The paper proves that surjective isometries between unit spheres of ℓ^p-direct sums of strictly convex Banach spaces extend to linear (real) or linear/conjugate-linear (complex) isometries on the whole space.
motivation: Mazur–Ulam-type extension problems (whether sphere isometries extend to global isometries) are a classical theme in Banach space geometry, and the authors aim to extend known results to ℓ^p-direct sums under weak hypotheses on the summands.
method: Functional-analytic techniques: analysis of the extreme/unit structure of direct sums, strictly convex summands, and differentiability of the norm to construct linear extensions of sphere isometries.
result: Every surjective isometry between the unit spheres of the considered ℓ^p-direct sums extends to a global isometry, with endpoint cases yielding a Mazur–Ulam property for the real absolutely continuous space with the sum norm.
conclusion: The extension theorem generalizes prior Mazur–Ulam-type results to ℓ^p-direct sums, with separate treatment of endpoint exponents and a discussion of Lipschitz/differentiable function spaces.

title: Numerical Analysis For A Nonlinear Coupled Thermoelastic System With Acoustic Boundary Conditions
authors: Adriano A. Alc\^antara, Bruno A. Carmo, Juan B. L\'imaco, Carlos M. Guzm\'an
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the first [MATH]-norm error analysis for a nonlinear thermoelastic system with acoustic boundary conditions. The model involves three coupled variables: the acoustic potential [MATH], the temperature [MATH], and the normal displacement to the boundary [MATH], with nonlinearities [MATH] in the domain and [MATH] on the boundary, in addition to a nonlocal term [MATH] in the heat equation. We establish error estimates for the fully discrete problem, using the Crank-Nicolson method for time discretization and finite element method with basis of degree [MATH] for space discretization. We demonstrate that the domain-boundary coupling induces a half-power loss in the spatial convergence order for the variable [MATH], and this effect propagates to the remaining variables due to the thermoelastic and boundary couplings, resulting in the final error estimate [MATH]. A bootstrap argument is employed to ensure the uniform boundedness of [MATH], which is essential for handling the nonlinearity. Numerical results using Lagrange finite element basis of degrees [MATH] (linear, quadratic, and cubic) corroborate the theoretical estimates and illustrate the transition from suboptimal to optimal convergence orders when the exact solution possesses additional [MATH] regularity.
tldr: The paper provides a numerical error analysis for a nonlinear coupled thermoelastic system with acoustic boundary conditions using finite elements and Crank-Nicolson time discretization.
motivation: The authors aim to establish convergence estimates for a fully discrete nonlinear thermoelastic-acoustic model with domain and boundary nonlinearities, including a nonlocal term in the heat equation.
method: They use Crank-Nicolson time stepping and finite element discretization with Lagrange basis functions of degree k, employing a bootstrap argument to control the nonlinearity and derive error bounds.
result: They show that domain-boundary coupling causes a half-power loss in the spatial convergence order for the acoustic potential, which propagates to the other variables, yielding a suboptimal overall error estimate.
conclusion: Numerical experiments with linear, quadratic, and cubic elements corroborate the theoretical convergence rates and exhibit a transition to optimal orders when the exact solution has extra regularity.

title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks For Loss-of-Control Risks
authors: John Kitaoka, Thao Amelia Pham, Carlos Rafael Giudice, Jacob Merizian
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
tldr: The paper introduces MiniLab, a synthetic multi-service environment for red-teaming covert distributed attacks by collaborating AI agents, and shows that single-trajectory monitors fail to detect them.
motivation: As AI agents proliferate and collaborate, control measures must stay effective when agents covertly collude toward harmful objectives; existing evaluations focus on single-agent side tasks rather than coordinated, distributed misbehavior.
method: The authors build MiniLab (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives, 16 human-optimized attacks) adapted from internal deployment infrastructure, and measure detection rates of a frontier monitor (GPT-5.6 Sol) on individual versus distributed attack trajectories, also testing model-planned attacks.
result: A monitor reading agents separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks versus 87% for the same side task in a single agent; individual unflagged attacks can be composed into longer loss-of-control sequences, and the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly at most 25% of the time versus 80% for human-crafted plans.
conclusion: Turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions To Correlated Bidders Via Neural Network Interpolation
authors: Mingyu Guo, Jiayuan Liu, Vincent Conitzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.
tldr: The paper proposes a neural-network-based empirical pipeline for designing revenue-maximizing, strategy-proof single-item auctions with correlated bidders, where exact optimal design is NP-hard.
motivation: Myerson's optimal auction theory covers independent bidders, but extending to correlated bidders yields non-monotonic allocations that break strategy-proofness, and optimal design there is computationally intractable, so practical methods are needed.
method: The authors interpolate Myerson's greedy marginal-profit allocation with neural networks, apply formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and add a constructive repair procedure, benchmarked against manual and neural baselines.
result: The approach attains near-optimal revenue across synthetic, adversarial, and real-world datasets, often shrinking the revenue gap by an order of magnitude, and introduces greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for benchmarking.
conclusion: Neural interpolation with verification offers a practical standard for optimal auction design in theoretically hard correlated settings, extensible to multi-unit auctions and integrable with RegretNet.

title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring The Safeguards Of Llm Options-Trading Agents
authors: Nitesh Saxena Mengxiao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.
tldr: A measurement study of 26 LLM-based options-trading agents (including 8 broker-native interfaces) scoring their robustness and security safeguards and the worst-case losses reachable through their documented order paths.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly place real options orders at retail brokers, and open-source agent projects proliferate far faster than they are audited; prior security work only examined academic equity-trading designs and only asked whether an attacker could flip a buy/sell decision.
method: Screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and literature to obtain 215 eligible repositories plus 8 broker-native agent interfaces, then scored 26 systems on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence.
result: Only 10 of 22 order-placing systems enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, none of the 26 authenticate text sources or cross-check market data, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step, and 13 (including 6 of 8 broker interfaces) can reach unbounded loss.
conclusion: Because an attacker controlling the agent's inputs can shift strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while keeping order direction correct, options agents require loss limits enforced at the order boundary rather than inside the model.

title: Computational Complexity And Exact Algorithms For Pressure-Driven Hydrogen Charging
authors: Nanase Sato, Wei Wu, Mutsunori Yagiura
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of deciding the feasibility of pressure-driven hydrogen charging from supply cylinders to demand cylinders without replenishment, asking whether an order of transfers allows every demand cylinder to reach its target pressure. Hydrogen can be transferred from a cylinder to another only when the supply cylinder has higher pressure than the demand cylinder. The charging to each demand cylinder must be completed before starting another, and each transfer continues until the connected cylinders reach equal pressures or the demand cylinder reaches its target. We consider equal-capacity supply cylinders and arbitrary positive rational demand cylinder capacities. Let [MATH] be the number of demand cylinders and [MATH] the binary input length. With one supply cylinder, feasibility is decidable in polynomial time; with two, it is NP-complete even with cylinder capacities equal to [MATH] and nonnegative integer pressures. We prove that feasibility is preserved even if the supply cylinders are always used in non-decreasing order of their current pressures when filling each demand cylinder. We also show that majorization of residual supply cylinder pressure states justifies discarding majorized states in dynamic programming over sets of completed demand cylinders without losing any feasible remaining demand cylinder order. With two supply cylinders, one state per completed demand cylinder set suffices, yielding [MATH] time and space. With three, the exponential time hypothesis (ETH) excludes deterministic [MATH]-time algorithms. This lower bound is tight in the exponent because the rule for order of supply cylinders allows feasibility to be decided in [MATH] time by enumerating only demand cylinder orders.
tldr: A classical complexity-theoretic study of deciding feasibility of pressure-driven hydrogen charging schedules among supply and demand cylinders.
motivation: Hydrogen refueling via cascaded pressure-driven transfers raises a natural algorithmic question: can an order of transfers be found that brings every demand cylinder to its target pressure without replenishment?
method: The authors characterize feasibility for one, two, and three equal-capacity supply cylinders with rational demand capacities, prove NP-completeness for two cylinders, and develop dynamic programming over sets of completed demand cylinders justified by a majorization argument on residual pressure states.
result: With one supply cylinder feasibility is polynomial-time decidable; with two it is NP-complete but solvable in O^*(2^M) time and space via majorization-pruned DP; with three, ETH rules out deterministic subexponential algorithms, and a matching upper bound follows from enumerating demand orders.
conclusion: The work gives a tight complexity classification and exact exponential algorithms for pressure-driven hydrogen charging, with majorization as the key pruning principle.

title: Tactix: Towards A Programmable Strategy Interface For Flexible Sat Solving
authors: Haoze Wu, Andr\'e Schidler, Armin Biere, Nina Narodytska
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
tldr: Tactix is a proof-producing CDCL SAT solver that cleanly separates proof rules from solving strategies, exposing a programmable interface for designing and evaluating new strategies.
motivation: In modern SAT solvers, strategies are tightly coupled to internal implementations, making it hard to define and test new strategies without modifying solver internals.
method: The authors build a sequential CDCL solver incorporating a wide range of state-of-the-art techniques with a modular interface allowing users to invoke individual techniques, observe their effects, and program custom strategies; they also document an AI-assisted development process.
result: Tactix's default programmable strategy outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on 2024–2026 SAT Competition benchmarks, and domain-tailored strategies derived via the interface yield gains over strong baselines.
conclusion: Tactix is intended as reusable infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel SAT solving strategies, with a self-study of AI-assisted software development.

title: Information Theory Of Random Composition Trees
authors: Doron Sivan, Weishun Zhong, Tankut Can, Mikhail Katkov, Misha Tsodyks
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random composition trees model the hierarchical semantic structures of meaningful texts as a statistical ensemble generated by recursively splitting texts into coherent chunks. A recent study shows that different text types can be described by random composition trees with distinct branching factors, and that the entropy rates of these trees exhibit a similar dependence across text types as the entropy rates of the actual texts. Motivated by this correspondence, we analyze information-theoretic properties of this stochastic splitting model. First, we demonstrate that the entropy of random composition trees grows linearly with the root size, and we derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. Second, we prove that large trees exhibit typicality: with high probability, they belong to a typical set in which each tree is approximately equally likely. Our analysis reveals that the random composition tree model shares two key information-theoretic properties of language when modeled as a stationary and ergodic stochastic process: linear entropy growth and typicality.
tldr: The paper analyzes information-theoretic properties of random composition trees used to model hierarchical semantic structures in texts, showing linear entropy growth and typicality.
motivation: Motivated by a correspondence between entropy rates of random composition trees and actual texts, the authors study whether this stochastic splitting model shares key information-theoretic properties of language.
method: They derive analytical expressions for the entropy and entropy rate of random composition trees as functions of root size and branching factor, and prove a typicality result for large trees.
result: The entropy grows linearly with root size, and with high probability large trees belong to a typical set where each tree is approximately equally likely.
conclusion: Random composition trees exhibit linear entropy growth and typicality, mirroring two key information-theoretic properties of language modeled as a stationary ergodic process.

title: From Trust Scores To Driver Decisions: An Abstaining Evidential Decision Layer For Event Validation In VANETs
authors: \.ipek Abas{\i}kele\c{s} Turgut
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trust management in vehicular ad hoc networks is highly active, yet the decision that a driver needs, whether a reported event is real, has received far less attention; the schemes that make it force every decision into two outcomes, even on thin or conflicting evidence. This paper presents CREST, a vehicle-side event-decision framework that can withhold a decision its evidence does not support. Each vehicle weights the reports it holds by the trust, proximity and freshness of their senders, fuses them with Yager's rule, and decides only when the fused margin reaches an abstention threshold. Abstention is a waiting state: a vehicle still unsure at the event is resolved by an explicit application policy, which makes the trade-off between missed hazards and unnecessary detours visible. CREST requires only a scalar trust per reporter and is built here on an evidential trust model whose consensus and revocation steps are updated to support the decision layer. A single report is shown to change the decision margin by at most its weight, which bounds the influence of an attacker coalition by its trust. In a pre-registered simulation study with fourteen attacks, including position spoofing and trust-gated camouflage, and with all unspecified parameters of all systems tuned by the same procedure, CREST reduces the decision error of two published trust-based dissemination systems from 0.162 and 0.106 to 0.051. With the best-guess policy it also lowers both missed and unnecessary reroutes and outperforms the forced binary rule on both error types in every cell.
tldr: CREST is a vehicle-side decision layer for VANET event validation that abstains when fused evidence is insufficient, using trust-weighted reports combined with Yager's rule.
motivation: Existing trust-management schemes in vehicular networks force binary real/fake decisions even when reports are sparse or conflicting, producing avoidable missed hazards or unnecessary reroutes.
method: Each vehicle weights received reports by sender trust, proximity, and freshness, fuses them via Yager's rule, and decides only when the fused margin exceeds an abstention threshold; unresolved cases are settled by an explicit application policy, built on an evidential trust model with updated consensus and revocation steps.
result: A single report shifts the decision margin by at most its weight, bounding attacker-coalition influence by trust; in a pre-registered simulation with fourteen attacks, decision error drops from 0.162 and 0.106 (two published systems) to 0.051, with fewer false alarms and missed reroutes than the forced binary rule.
conclusion: Explicit abstention with an evidential decision layer improves reliability of event validation in VANETs and makes the missed-hazard versus detour trade-off transparent.

title: The Missing Compliance Class: Llm Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, And A Free Check
authors: Ruqiya Bin Safi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.
tldr: The paper shows that LLM-based jailbreak graders suffer from a 'class collapse' in which compliant responses are systematically mislabeled as evasions, and proposes a cheap diagnostic plus a minimum reporting standard.
motivation: Jailbreak attack success rates are typically reported as intrinsic properties of target models, but the grader itself can distort these numbers; the authors aim to quantify and expose this grader-induced bias.
method: Holding target model, prompts, and responses fixed, the authors swap in several 8B–9B dense graders from different model families and compare per-class label counts, compliance rates, and non-refusal rates across multiple corpora.
result: Three collapsing graders map compliant responses into the neighboring 'evasion' class, one never assigning the compliance label across 900 responses; compliance rates then differ by factors of 22–25 across graders, versus 1.7–2.8 without the collapsing graders.
conclusion: Per-class label counts provide a free, label-free diagnostic of grader collapse, and the authors recommend reporting compliance rate with its class counts and named grader alongside the additive non-refusal rate.

title: Improved Approximation And Tight Competition For Simple Auctions
authors: Yichen Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for [MATH] items are independent. Write [MATH] for optimal revenue, [MATH] and [MATH] for the revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and [MATH] for grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove [MATH]. This establishes tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling under regularity and answers an open question from Beyhaghi et al. (EC 2025). For general independent items, we prove [MATH]. This improves the previous approximation factors of [MATH] from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and [MATH] from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). On the lower bound side, we construct an instance in which prices for three disjoint bundles earn more than [MATH], improving the previous lower bound of [MATH] from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). We also show that exact recovery of one buyer's optimal revenue by the better of separate selling and bundling requires [MATH] bidders in the worst case.
tldr: This paper studies simple auctions for one additive buyer with independent item values, proving improved revenue approximation and competition guarantees for bundling versus separate selling.
motivation: Simple auctions such as separate selling and grand bundling are practically important, but tight approximation and competition guarantees for these mechanisms under independent regular items were not fully established.
method: The author proves revenue inequalities comparing optimal revenue with separate selling, grand bundling, and grand-bundle second-price revenue with two bidders, and constructs lower-bound instances for multi-bundle pricing.
result: For independent regular items, tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling are established, answering an open question; for general independent items, improved approximation factors are obtained, along with an improved lower bound for three disjoint bundles and a bidder-count requirement for exact recovery.
conclusion: The work sharpens the theoretical understanding of simple auction performance, but it is in algorithmic game theory and mechanism design rather than quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Non-Monetary Mechanisms For Stochastic Scheduling Via Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensation
authors: David X. Lin, Chido Onyeze, Giannis Fikioris, Siddhartha Banerjee, \'eva Tardos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can a shared resource be allocated without money when agents have private, stochastic demands that can be queued for a while, and may behave strategically, or even adversarially? We introduce a paradigm for non-monetary online resource allocation called Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensator (SPEC). Our objective is to guarantee each agent a large fraction of its ideal utility: an individual benchmark corresponding to serving the highest-valued fraction of its demand permitted by an equal share of capacity. We seek guarantees that hold regardless of other agents' behavior, including potentially adversarial and collusive behavior. Our approach builds on the idea of pairwise externality compensation, making it computationally efficient by replacing exact calculations of future externalities with sampled estimates. The central insight is that local mixing, exploited through coupled simulations, allows these estimates to be computed efficiently while preserving robust utility guarantees. In our main technical contribution, we instantiate SPEC in a stochastic scheduling model in which agents receive jobs with private values, unserved jobs persist across periods subject to random expiration, and a single server processes at most one job per period. Our mechanism gives each agent a simple strategy that achieves the optimal worst-case fraction of ideal utility available to a fully informed planner, up to a sublinear additive loss in total utility. We also show that this fraction approaches [MATH] in the long-horizon limit as the expiration probability vanishes: sufficiently persistent jobs allow each agent to secure nearly its full ideal utility. The mechanism runs in [MATH] expected amortized time per period, where [MATH] is the number of agents; significantly, the expected amortized computational overhead per period is independent of the time horizon [MATH].
tldr: The paper proposes SPEC, a non-monetary online mechanism that compensates agents for pairwise externalities estimated via coupled simulations, guaranteeing each agent a large fraction of its ideal utility under strategic or adversarial behavior in a stochastic queuing/scheduling model.
motivation: Shared resources often must be allocated without money, yet agents have private stochastic demands, jobs that persist across periods, and may act strategically or collusively, so robust worst-case utility guarantees are needed that do not rely on monetary transfers or truthful reporting.
method: The authors build on pairwise externality compensation, replacing exact future-externality computations with sampled estimates computed efficiently through local mixing and coupled simulations; they instantiate the scheme in a stochastic scheduling model with a single server, private job values, and random expiration.
result: Each agent has a simple strategy achieving the optimal worst-case fraction of ideal utility up to sublinear additive loss, this fraction approaches 1 in the long-horizon limit as expiration probability vanishes, and the mechanism runs in expected amortized time per period independent of the time horizon.
conclusion: Sampled pairwise externality compensation enables computationally efficient, strategy-robust non-monetary resource allocation with strong individual guarantees, showing that persistent jobs allow agents to secure nearly full ideal utility.

title: Towards End-to-End Privacy-Preserving Ai For Real-Time Ecg Monitoring
authors: Beyazit Bestami Yuksel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Healthcare artificial intelligence is shifting from centralized archives toward distributed pipelines that combine wearables, edge processing, cloud analytics, and multi-institutional learning. In this regime, electrocardiogram (ECG) streams cross multiple trust boundaries, so privacy cannot be reduced to a single transmission control. Existing privacy-enhancing technologies typically secure isolated stages and leave gaps between acquisition, analysis, and institutional collaboration. This doctoral research develops a unified lifecycle framework for end-to-end privacy-preserving ECG AI. Rather than introducing another privacy mechanism, it orchestrates complementary privacy-enhancing technologies across the clinical ECG lifecycle, allocating each mechanism to the trust boundary where its security, computational, and operational properties are most appropriate. Three interoperable modules instantiate the framework: AES with CKKS-based homomorphic statistics for secure monitoring; adaptive chaotic protection for low-latency edge transmission; and federated learning with homomorphic aggregation under heterogeneous partitions. Across prototype monitoring, signal-security analysis, and simulated collaboration, the programme shows that privacy layers can be composed without collapsing diagnostic utility, while exposing overhead and fidelity limits that constrain clinical translation.
tldr: This doctoral research proposes a lifecycle framework that composes homomorphic encryption, chaotic edge protection, and federated learning to preserve privacy in real-time ECG AI pipelines.
motivation: ECG data increasingly flow through distributed clinical and wearable pipelines, crossing multiple trust boundaries where existing privacy mechanisms secure only isolated stages.
method: The framework orchestrates complementary privacy-enhancing technologies across acquisition, edge transmission, cloud analytics, and multi-institutional learning, instantiating three modules with AES/CKKS homomorphic statistics, adaptive chaotic protection, and federated learning with homomorphic aggregation.
result: Prototype and simulation studies indicate that privacy layers can be composed without collapsing diagnostic utility, while revealing overhead and fidelity limits for clinical translation.
conclusion: End-to-end privacy for ECG AI requires trust-boundary-aware orchestration of privacy mechanisms rather than a single transmission control, though practical overheads remain.

title: How Much Feedback Is Needed To Break Template Protection? The Geometric Vulnerability Of Biometric Authentication
authors: Eliron Rahimi, Margarita Osadchy, Orr Dunkelman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biometric authentication systems increasingly use privacy-preserving mechanisms to protect sensitive templates. However, the authentication interface itself may still leak information that enables reconstruction attacks. Prior attacks exploit released similarity scores, whereas more advanced systems reveal only the binary accept/reject decision. This binary feedback provides substantially less information, making template reconstruction far more challenging. In this work, we introduce query-efficient reconstruction attacks under extremely limited feedback, addressing two key limitations of prior attacks. First, we introduce the first attack that reconstructs protected biometric templates using only authentication success/failure feedback by exploiting the geometric constraints of biometric authentication. Second, we introduce distribution-aware query-efficient reconstruction methods for score-releasing systems, achieving a more realistic threat model by reducing the number of required queries by a factor of [MATH] compared to recent prior score-based attacks. Finally, we combine these two insights by incorporating a pretrained facial diffusion prior into our geometric binary attack, reducing the number of required queries by a factor of [MATH]. Our findings reveal a fundamental security limitation of biometric authentication: independently of the template protection mechanism, the authentication process itself exposes geometric information that can enable perfect template reconstruction up to numerical precision. Moreover, the distribution of biometric templates can be leveraged to make significantly more effective reconstruction attacks.
tldr: The paper introduces query-efficient reconstruction attacks that recover protected biometric templates from only binary accept/reject authentication feedback, using the geometry of the authentication decision boundary and a pretrained facial diffusion prior.
motivation: Privacy-preserving biometric template protection is often assumed safe, but the authentication interface itself may leak information; prior attacks required similarity scores, so it was unclear how much weaker binary-only feedback is as a side channel.
method: The authors formulate template reconstruction as solving geometric constraints induced by accept/reject regions, develop distribution-aware, query-efficient querying strategies for score-releasing systems, and augment the binary geometric attack with a pretrained facial diffusion prior.
result: Binary-feedback attacks achieve perfect template reconstruction up to numerical precision, and the distribution-aware and diffusion-prior variants reduce the required number of queries by large factors relative to prior score-based attacks.
conclusion: The authentication process itself, independent of the template protection mechanism, fundamentally exposes geometric information enabling template reconstruction, so biometric systems need to treat the decision interface as a leakage channel.

title: Residual Carleman Lift For Nonlinear Lattice Boltzmann Simulations
authors: Ilya Karlin
