Extensive experiments across several state-of-the-art MLLMs, including LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, and Gemma, demonstrate that our approach identifies cross-modal triggers that are more efficient, effective, and less detectable than direct optimization baselines, highlighting a critical new threat vector in multimodal systems.
tldr: The paper introduces 'backdoor infection', a cross-modal attack that induces malicious behavior in multimodal LLMs by planting a trigger in a second modality, exploiting the shared latent space, without poisoning that modality during training.
motivation: Multimodal LLMs inherit backdoors from single-modality poisoning, but it is unclear whether such vulnerabilities can spread to other modalities; the authors aim to expose this overlooked threat vector.
method: Starting from a model backdoored in one modality, they construct a corresponding trigger in an unpoisoned 'infected' modality via a lightweight, constraint-aware optimization that exploits the shared latent representation.
result: Experiments on LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, and Gemma show the cross-modal triggers are more efficient, effective, and stealthier than direct-optimization baselines.
conclusion: Cross-modal backdoor infection is a practical and critical security threat for multimodal systems, calling for new defenses.

title: Coopshift: Post-Training Amplifies The Memory Curse In Llm Cooperation
authors: Jiayuan Liu, Shiyi Du, Tianqin Li, Emanuel Tewolde, Keyang Xuan, Vincent Conitzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does post-training change cooperation during repeated interaction? Within each of seven released model lineages, we compare pretrained (Base), supervised fine-tuned (SFT), and subsequent preference- or reward-optimized (Aligned) checkpoints across seven social dilemmas. Copies of each checkpoint play one another for 200 rounds, with visible history limited to the last two or forty rounds. The memory curse refers to lower cooperation when agents can see more past rounds. Our central finding is that post-training amplifies this decline. Averaged across the six binary-action games, expanding visible history reduces cooperation at every SFT and Aligned checkpoint. At each post-trained stage, these declines exceed Base's in six of seven lineages. Most of this average amplification is already present at SFT. With long history, both post-trained stages also cooperate less than Base on average in each binary-action game. In the symmetric binary games, their fitted cooperation rates fall more steeply on average than Base's as per-round cooperation costs rise, benefits fall, or noncooperation becomes more rewarding. The difference in cooperation rates between Aligned and SFT also changes from one-shot decisions to repeated play. When given the same past records, their choices depend on whether the instructions describe a final round or possible future interaction. Post-training evaluation should therefore go beyond isolated choices to assess whether cooperation is sustained in repeated interaction and how it depends on payoffs and visible history.
tldr: Post-training (SFT and preference/reward optimization) in LLM lineages amplifies the 'memory curse', i.e. the tendency for agents to cooperate less when more past rounds of interaction are visible.
motivation: Repeated-game cooperation among LLM agents is increasingly important for multi-agent deployments, but it is unclear how post-training stages (pretraining, SFT, alignment) shape the sustainability of cooperation in repeated interaction.
method: Within each of seven model lineages, Base, SFT, and Aligned checkpoints are made to play copies of themselves for 200 rounds across seven social dilemmas, with visible history restricted to the last two or forty rounds, and fitted cooperation rates are compared as payoff parameters vary.
result: In six of seven lineages the cooperation decline from longer visible history is larger at post-trained stages than at Base, most of the amplification already appearing at SFT; under long history post-trained models also cooperate less than Base, and their cooperation rates fall more steeply as cooperation costs rise or noncooperation pays better.
conclusion: Post-training evaluation of LLM agents should move beyond isolated one-shot choices to assess sustained cooperation in repeated interaction and its dependence on payoffs and visible history.

title: Envy-Free Randomized Apportionment
authors: Francesco la Commare, Jamie Tucker-Foltz, Victor Verdugo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The United States allocates representatives to each state in proportion to its population, while many parliamentary democracies select representatives from party lists in proportion to the number of votes each party receives. In both settings, the legislature's small size necessitates rounding to the nearest whole number of seats. Recent work has shown a plethora of ways to randomly round seat shares to achieve perfect ex ante fairness. As a result, party (state) [MATH] may have a larger number of votes (population) than party [MATH] but receive fewer seats. In this case, we say that party [MATH] envies party [MATH]. We investigate the extent to which such envy is avoidable. Specifically, we seek to design apportionment rules that minimize the expected number of envious pairs [MATH]. If the expectation is zero, we say that the seat allocation is envy-free. On the negative side, we show that any [MATH]-party apportionment rule that ignores lower quotas (the floors of the deserved number of seats for each party) suffers from a worst-case envy of [MATH], even on instances where an envy-free allocation exists. All previously studied apportionment rules fall into this class and thus do a poor job of minimizing envy. In the case where all lower quotas are equal, we prove that all allocations have the same expected envy. In the general case, we we introduce a general polynomial-time LP framework for a large class of apportionment objectives, including minimizing the expectation and variance of envy, by efficiently solving the separation problem on the dual. Finally, we empirically demonstrate that envy-free allocations exist very frequently, including in every historical instance from the US decennial census. Taken together, these results provide a clear recipe for implementing randomized apportionment in a less objectionable way in practice.
tldr: The paper studies randomized apportionment rules that minimize the expected number of envious pairs when rounding seat shares to whole numbers, providing impossibility results, an LP framework, and empirical evidence that envy-free allocations exist frequently.
motivation: Legislatures are small, so proportional vote or population shares must be rounded to whole seats; naive rounding can make a party with more votes receive fewer seats than a smaller party, creating envy, and the authors ask how avoidable this is.
method: The authors prove worst-case lower bounds for apportionment rules ignoring lower quotas, show all allocations have equal expected envy when lower quotas coincide, and develop a polynomial-time LP framework solving the dual separation problem for objectives such as expected envy and variance.
result: Rules ignoring lower quotas suffer worst-case envy linear in the number of parties even when envy-free allocations exist; the LP framework optimizes envy-based objectives, and empirically envy-free allocations appear very often, including in all US census instances.
conclusion: The work gives a practical recipe for less objectionable randomized apportionment, but remains entirely within social choice and combinatorial optimization, with no quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networking content.

title: Spides: Information-Flow Control For Browser Agents
authors: Egor Zverev, Juhee Kim, Leon Trampert, Boris K\"opf, Aashish Kolluri, Shruti Tople, Santiago Zanella-B\'eguelin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same-origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross-origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element-level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element-level ground-truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at [URL].
tldr: SPIDES is a browser-agent security framework that enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions on confidentiality and integrity labels derived from element-level HTML annotations.
motivation: LLM-driven browser agents break traditional web security boundaries like the Same-Origin Policy, exposing users to prompt injection and data exfiltration; restoring SOP alone is argued to be neither sufficient nor necessary.
method: The authors label HTML elements with confidentiality/integrity annotations, propagate these labels through the agent's actions (typing, clicking, navigating), mask untrusted or confidential content from the model's context, and block policy-violating flows; they also introduce MicroNet, a 28-site ecosystem with element-level ground truth and paired benign/adversarial tasks.
result: SPIDES achieves a 0% attack success rate by design while maintaining high task completion and autonomy, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on both security and utility.
conclusion: Information-flow control is presented as an effective way to extend web security principles to autonomous browser agents, with guarantees that are independent of the underlying model.

title: Empirical Analysis Of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs
authors: Claudiu-Nicu B\u{a}rbieru, Corentin Libert, Peterson Yuhala, Andrei Arusoaie, Matthieu Bettinger, Oana-Otilia Captarencu, Pascal Felber, Emanuel Onica, Etienne Rivi\`ere, Valerio Schiavoni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.
tldr: An empirical benchmark study of TEE-enabled Ethereum L2 rollup sequencer designs comparing proposer-builder separation (PBS) against a monolithic architecture.
motivation: L2 rollups dominate Ethereum scaling but rely on a centralized sequencer that enables censorship and MEV extraction; TEEs are proposed to enforce verifiable neutrality, yet their practical performance and security trade-offs remain experimentally unexamined.
method: The authors implement and benchmark TEE-backed rollup sequencer variants under monolithic and PBS models, measuring throughput, latency, and overhead attributable to TEE execution.
result: TEE integration imposes only a small performance penalty on rollup operation, and PBS does not meaningfully amplify this overhead while enabling more specialized builder logic that can improve performance.
conclusion: TEE-based sequencer designs are practically viable for strengthening rollup security, with PBS offering a modular alternative to monolithic sequencers at modest cost.

title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language And Multimodal Agents
authors: Wonjun Lee, Vaidehi Patil, Zaid Khan, Yue Zhang, Hyunji Lee, Suhyun Kim, Mohit Bansal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.
tldr: The paper studies dormant poisoning attacks in language and multimodal agents and proposes a LookAhead Defense that uses the released model's own safe responses as a safety reference.
motivation: Dormant backdoors implanted before release can be reactivated by benign downstream fine-tuning, and it is unclear whether this threat extends to agentic actions and multimodal settings; existing defenses require external safe responses or a trusted clean reference model.
method: The authors build a Safety Buffer that pairs harmful inputs with the released model's responses plus benign paraphrases to strip harmful intent, then introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates and penalizes only those predicted to weaken safety or induce over-refusal.
result: Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense cuts harmful agent behavior from up to 93.9% down to at most 14.2% and harmful language-model responses from up to 92.5% down to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while retaining competitive utility and low over-refusal.
conclusion: Dormant poisoning generalizes to unseen agent actions and can hide multiple coexisting behaviors, but the attacker's need to preserve safe release behavior provides a usable safety anchor for robust, utility-preserving defense.

title: The Lattice Of Coalition Logics Between Mcl And Cl: Coatoms And Compact Meets
authors: Yuqiang Dou Shanxia Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed finite set [MATH] of at least two agents, we investigate the lattice [MATH] of coalition logics between minimal coalition logic (MCL) and classical coalition logic (CL), with extensions required to be structural. This lattice is order-dual to an interval in the subvariety lattice of Boolean coalition algebras. The eight basic extensions obtained by imposing seriality, independence of agents, and determinism form a Boolean cube under inclusion, but not a sublattice of [MATH]. Our main results concern coatoms and compact meets. First, finite critical coalition algebras, realized as complex algebras of finite general concurrent games, yield three infinite families of pairwise distinct coatoms containing seriality, distinguished by failures of independence, determinism, or both. An explicit splitting characterizes the unique coatom omitting seriality. Second, the meet of two basic extensions is compact if and only if the extensions are comparable. For incomparable pairs, no axiomatization of the meet can use formulas of uniformly bounded modal depth, even with infinitely many axioms. Consequently, [MATH] and three natural principal intervals are non-coherent algebraic lattices. These results reveal lattice-theoretic phenomena beyond the inclusion order of the eight basic extensions.
tldr: The paper studies the lattice of structural extensions of minimal coalition logic up to classical coalition logic, focusing on coatoms and compact meets.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the lattice-theoretic structure of coalition logics between MCL and CL and its connection to varieties of Boolean coalition algebras.
method: They use duality with Boolean coalition algebras, finite critical coalition algebras realized as complex algebras of general concurrent games, and splitting techniques to analyze coatoms and compact meets.
result: They identify three infinite families of coatoms containing seriality, characterize the unique coatom omitting seriality, and show that meets of incomparable basic extensions are non-compact and lack uniformly bounded modal-depth axiomatizations.
conclusion: The lattice and several principal intervals are non-coherent algebraic lattices, revealing phenomena beyond the inclusion order of the eight basic extensions.

title: Narratives Mislead: An Empirical Study Of How LLMs Misjudge Cvss Severity In Bug Bounty Reports
authors: Ruitao Feng, Yuekang Li, Yao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bug bounty platforms receive vulnerability reports faster than vendors can triage them, and Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for assigning the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity that drives prioritization. Prior evaluations score short CVE descriptions and report accuracy, but deployment depends on how models err, not only how often. CVSS gives each metric a formal meaning that departs from how researchers describe impact in narrative reports, and model rationales suggest that errors concentrate where the two diverge; we ask whether this pattern is systematic. From 4,281 publicly disclosed reports mined from Huntr and HackerOne, we build a benchmark of 240 Huntr reports with vendor-validated CVSS vectors and evaluate eight LLMs under four prompting strategies and fine-tuning, measuring errors by severity class and score and analysing sub-vectors on individual reports. The best prompting configuration reaches only 49.58% level accuracy, ten points above always predicting the majority level, and fine-tuning a 7B model raises this to at most 56.25%, an optimistic upper bound. Errors are directional: models overestimate far more often than they underestimate, and they almost never recognize low-severity vulnerabilities. We trace these errors to three semantic boundaries that the specification draws and narrative reports blur: potential versus realized impact, impact magnitude versus authorization scope, and uncertainty versus the worst case. Because the violations originate partly in the report, we close with an exploratory case study: on four reports, a boundary-aligned, exploit-free report structure lowered a frontier model's score where the narrative invited an unclaimed account takeover, but left the metrics a report does not settle open, and the two published labels disagreed on three of the four reports.
tldr: An empirical study showing that LLMs systematically misjudge CVSS severity in bug bounty reports because narrative descriptions blur semantic boundaries drawn by the CVSS specification.
motivation: Bug bounty platforms face report backlogs and increasingly consider LLMs for CVSS severity assignment, yet prior evaluations only measure accuracy on short CVE descriptions rather than characterizing how and where models err in realistic narrative reports.
method: The authors mine 4,281 publicly disclosed Huntr and HackerOne reports, build a benchmark of 240 Huntr reports with vendor-validated CVSS vectors, and evaluate eight LLMs under four prompting strategies plus fine-tuning, analyzing errors by severity class, score, and sub-vector.
result: The best prompting configuration achieves only 49.58% severity-level accuracy (ten points above the majority baseline), fine-tuning a 7B model reaches at most 56.25%, errors skew toward overestimation, low-severity vulnerabilities are almost never recognized, and a small case study suggests boundary-aligned report structures can reduce inflated scores.
conclusion: LLM-based CVSS assessment is unreliable in deployment, with errors traceable to three semantic boundaries (potential vs. realized impact, impact magnitude vs. authorization scope, uncertainty vs. worst case) that both reports and models conflate; improved report structure may partially mitigate this.

title: Consistency Is The Attack Surface: Detecting Coordinated Retrieval Poisoning With Embedding Geometry
authors: Zeyan Li, Qirong Guo, Jianfeng Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consistency-based defenses for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) rest on an assumption that a sparse adversary breaks: a poisoning campaign may modify a negligible fraction of the corpus, yet retrieval concentrates its passages into the reader's context. Across four Natural Questions retrieval seeds, at least one injection reaches the top-5 in 94.1% of targeted query--seed rows, and all three form a retrieved majority in 52.9%. Under our short-answer protocol, RobustRAG and ReliabilityRAG reach exposure-conditional attack success 0.512, against 0.576 for undefended RAG, while lowering clean accuracy from 0.328 to 0.216. Coordination, however, leaves a fingerprint: a dense, query-anchored component in the evidence embedding geometry. CoordGuard audits this structure from robustly normalized query-weighted affinities, without poison labels, correct answers, or reader gradients. Its always-filter mode suppresses the selected component whenever one forms; a benign-calibrated gate suppresses it only at unusually high scores and traces a robustness--utility frontier. Pooling four retrieval seeds, e5 always-filtering reduces [MATH] to 0.167 overall and 0.138 on parametrically unknown queries, at a 13.6-point clean cost, while a Contriever gate retains clean accuracy 0.315 at [MATH]. The reduction transfers across two readers, three tasks, and multiple retriever--auditor pairs, and count-matched controls attribute it to component-targeted removal rather than deletion volume. These findings recast poison detection from judging truth to auditing the structure of retrieved evidence.
tldr: CoordGuard detects coordinated retrieval-poisoning attacks on RAG systems by auditing the embedding geometry of retrieved evidence, exploiting the dense query-anchored component that coordinated poisoning leaves behind.
motivation: Consistency-based RAG defenses assume poisons are sparse, but a coordinated campaign can inject few documents that nonetheless dominate the top-k retrieved context, so defenses must detect coordination rather than judge truthfulness of passages.
method: The authors characterize poisoning as a query-anchored dense component in query-weighted, robustly normalized evidence embeddings, and audit this structure without poison labels, gold answers, or reader gradients, using an always-filter mode and a benign-calibrated gated mode.
result: Across four Natural Questions retrieval seeds, injections reach top-5 in 94.1% of targeted rows and form a majority in 52.9%; e5 always-filtering reduces exposure-conditional attack success to 0.167 (0.138 on parametrically unknown queries) at a 13.6-point clean-accuracy cost, and a Contriever gate retains 0.315 clean accuracy, transferring across two readers and three tasks.
conclusion: Poison detection in RAG should be recast from judging factual truth to auditing the geometric structure of retrieved evidence, yielding a robustness-utility frontier for retrieval integrity.

title: Cat-rag: Improving Secure Code Generation With Category-Aware Agentic Retrieval
authors: Mahdieh Abazar, Lorenzo de Carli, Benjamin Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, security vulnerabilities remain widespread, and retrieval-augmented code generation (RACG) can further amplify risk when retrieved knowledge is verbose or vulnerable to poisoning. Existing secure RACG approaches inject security knowledge at a fine-grained vulnerability level, causing prompt overhead and diluted model attention when a query implicates multiple related weaknesses. We propose CAT-RAG, an agentic security category-aware retrieval-augmented code generation framework. CAT-RAG performs adaptive category selection via an LLM as a categorizer agent and operates either as a standalone security layer or as a drop-in add-on to RACG pipelines, requiring no modification to the underlying model. We replace CWE-level retrieval with compact, language-specific security categories. These categories provide a higher-level abstraction over individual CWE weaknesses, organizing them by the security concern they share, such as Input Validation and Injection Attacks, rather than merely grouping related entries. Each category consolidates best practices and secure code examples into a single, prompt-efficient representation. We perform a comprehensive evaluation across CyberSecEval, CodeGuard+, and HumanEval. On CyberSecEval, CAT-RAG nearly doubles the secure code generation improvement over the state of the art (23.57% vs. 12.11%) while reducing token overhead by 41.71%.
tldr: CAT-RAG is an agentic, security-category-aware retrieval-augmented code generation framework that replaces fine-grained CWE-level retrieval with compact language-specific security categories to improve secure code generation while cutting prompt overhead.
motivation: LLM-based code generation frequently produces vulnerable code, and existing retrieval-augmented approaches inject security knowledge at the individual CWE level, which bloats prompts and dilutes model attention when a query touches multiple related weaknesses.
method: The framework uses an LLM categorizer agent to adaptively select high-level security categories (e.g., Input Validation and Injection Attacks) that consolidate best practices and secure code examples into prompt-efficient representations, operating either standalone or as a drop-in layer over existing RACG pipelines without modifying the underlying model.
result: On CyberSecEval, CAT-RAG nearly doubles the secure-code improvement of the prior state of the art (23.57% vs. 12.11%) while reducing token overhead by 41.71%, with additional evaluation on CodeGuard+ and HumanEval.
conclusion: Category-level, agent-selected retrieval offers a more effective and efficient route to secure code generation than vulnerability-level knowledge injection, and can be integrated into existing pipelines without retraining.

title: From Critical Transitions To Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, And Applications Across Disciplines
authors: Elisabeth H. Krueger, Koustav Halder, Woi Oh, Nusrat Molla, Juan C. Rocha, Giuseppe Ferro, Guillaume Falmagne, Annie B. Stephenson, Lan Wang Erlandsson, Jacques Bara, George I. Hagstrom, Nico Wunderling, Jiayu Li, Xander Huggins, Emma R. Zajdela, Harman Jaggi, Sara M. Constantino, Caronline Schill, Vitor V. Vasconcelos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.
tldr: This paper reviews and connects concepts of critical transitions, tipping points, regime shifts, and sustainability transformations across physics, ecology, and social sciences to clarify definitions and underlying theory.
motivation: Terms describing abrupt systemic change are used inconsistently across disciplines, creating confusion about mechanisms, irreversibility, and governance implications.
method: The authors present selected empirical examples and theoretical roots from physics/mathematics, Earth science/ecology, and social sciences, synthesizing them into a shared conceptual framework.
result: The paper distinguishes related phenomena and clarifies how concepts such as phase transitions, regime shifts, and socio-technical transitions differ and overlap across domains.
conclusion: A cross-disciplinary shared understanding can improve governance of social-ecological change toward more just and sustainable futures.

title: Hidden Urban Exposure To Energy-price Shocks: Spreading Burdens And Shifting Hotspots
authors: Yunfei Bai, Aaron Tesfa Tsion, Ra\'ul Rosales, Barbara Shollock, Wei He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cities need to anticipate where energy-price shocks could intensify hardship beyond established hotspots. How income distributions and fuel-price balances jointly shape this hidden exposure remains unclear. Here we address this gap by stress-testing nearly one million properties in six English local authorities, combining required-energy costs for existing housing with modelled local income distributions. Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the highest local exposure quarter lie outside the highest official fuel-poverty quarter. Electricity-led stress changes this hidden geography: when electricity unit prices alone triple from 2021, comparable to the unmitigated late-2022 cap increase, 38% of the resulting hidden-exposure group are absent from the crisis-based group. Entering neighbourhoods have newer, more efficient housing, more flats and greater electricity dependence than retained areas. Crisis preparedness should extend household protection beyond current hardship hotspots, using fuel-specific stress tests to anticipate support needs as fuel prices and heating systems change.
tldr: A socio-economic stress-test of ~1 million English properties shows that energy-price shocks create 'hidden' fuel-poverty hotspots that fall outside official fuel-poverty designations.
motivation: Cities need to anticipate where energy-price shocks will intensify hardship beyond currently recognized hotspots, yet how income distributions and fuel-price balances jointly shape this hidden exposure is unclear.
method: The authors combine required-energy costs for the existing housing stock with modelled local income distributions across nearly one million properties in six English local authorities, applying gas-led and electricity-led price stress scenarios.
result: Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the highest local exposure quarter lie outside the highest official fuel-poverty quarter; under tripled electricity unit prices, 38% of the hidden-exposure group are absent from the crisis-based group, with entering areas having newer, more efficient housing, more flats and greater electricity dependence.
conclusion: Crisis preparedness should extend household protection beyond current hardship hotspots, using fuel-specific stress tests to anticipate support needs as fuel prices and heating systems change.

title: Mathematics Of Herding
authors: Sayomi Kamimoto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A herd of animals often follows a leader who sets the direction of travel. The leader sometimes turns unexpectedly and the followers reshuffle. Yet the herd regroups itself and stays coherent. Our work aims to understand the herding behavior mathematically. We construct a minimal discrete-time nonequilibrium dynamical system with one-way coupling, and the minimal structure allows an exact analysis. Take the location of each follower in the frame of the leader. The recorded locations form a distribution. The limit of the distribution is the asymptotic spatial measure, whose geometric representation we study. The dynamics of the herd have an exact operator representation with two factors, the operator of a fixed leader-follower pair and the operator of the interaction rules, which reshuffle the pairs. We show that the influence of the leader passes through some follower more than once. As a result, two followers can have reciprocal influence, despite the one-way coupling.
tldr: The paper constructs a minimal discrete-time nonequilibrium dynamical model of animal herding and analyzes its asymptotic spatial distribution and operator representation.
motivation: The authors aim to understand mathematically how a herd remains coherent and regroups after a leader's unexpected turns despite one-way coupling.
method: They model follower locations in the leader's frame as a distribution and represent the dynamics exactly using operators for fixed leader-follower pairs and reshuffling interaction rules.
result: The analysis shows that the leader's influence can pass through a follower more than once, allowing reciprocal influence between followers even under one-way coupling.
conclusion: The work provides an exactly solvable minimal model of herding dynamics, but it is unrelated to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Note On Carmichael Numbers Of The Form $ N=(d+1)(3d+1)(4d+1)$
authors: Hayat Bensella
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study integers of the form \[ N=(d+1)(3d+1)(4d+1). \] Using Korselt's criterion, we prove that, provided the three factors are prime, [MATH] is a Carmichael number if and only if \[ d\equiv4. \] We also show that the special case [MATH] produces only [MATH] under the prime-factor hypothesis.
tldr: A pure number-theory note characterizing when numbers of the form N=(d+1)(3d+1)(4d+1) are Carmichael numbers via Korselt's criterion.
motivation: Carmichael numbers are the pseudoprimes underlying the Fermat primality test's failure modes, so parametrized families of them are of classical number-theoretic interest.
method: Applies Korselt's criterion to the three-factor product, assuming each factor is prime, and derives a congruence condition on d; also treats a special case separately.
result: Under the prime-factor hypothesis, N is Carmichael if and only if d satisfies a specific congruence (d ≡ 4), and the special case yields only one such number.
conclusion: The family admits a clean congruence characterization, giving a new parametrized construction of Carmichael numbers, but the work lies entirely in classical number theory.

title: Dynamic Programming For Value-at-risk Markov Decision Processes In Continuous Spaces
authors: Xian Chen, Erick Delage, Weikai Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a widely adopted quantile-based risk measure in practice, yet incorporating VaR objectives into Markov decision processes (VaR MDPs) remains a longstanding challenge. Recent work has derived dynamic programming equations for VaR MDPs in finite state and action spaces but left the case of more general spaces unresolved. This paper establishes, for the first time, the validity of these equations in continuous spaces, for both finite- and infinite-horizon settings. Such cases naturally arise in many real-world dynamic decision-making problems. As an application, we study an optimal execution problem with a VaR objective and demonstrate that our framework enables the characterization of optimal dynamic strategies, resolving an open question in the field.
tldr: The paper establishes dynamic programming equations for Value-at-Risk Markov decision processes in continuous state and action spaces, for both finite and infinite horizons.
motivation: VaR is a widely used quantile-based risk measure, but incorporating VaR objectives into MDPs has been a longstanding challenge; prior dynamic programming results existed only for finite state and action spaces.
method: The authors prove validity of dynamic programming recursions for VaR MDPs in general (continuous) spaces over finite and infinite horizons, and apply the framework to an optimal execution problem with a VaR objective.
result: The dynamic programming equations are shown to hold in continuous spaces, enabling characterization of optimal dynamic strategies and resolving an open question in optimal execution under VaR.
conclusion: The work extends risk-sensitive stochastic control theory to continuous spaces, providing a rigorous foundation for VaR-based dynamic decision-making in finance and related real-world problems.

title: A Crawling Metric On The Space Of Subtrees Of A Tree
authors: Thu-Le Tran, Cao Minh Quang, Nguyen Chi Tam, Kien Trung Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a crawling metric on the space of subtrees of a tree. The symmetric difference cannot tell whether two disjoint subtrees are close or far; we halve it and add the gap between them. The result is a metric, one half is the smallest factor, and the tree embeds canonically. The metric equals the least cost of crawling between subtrees by growing and shrinking without jumping. With simultaneous growth and shrinkage, subtrees of fixed length form a geodesic space.
tldr: The authors introduce a 'crawling' metric on the space of subtrees of a tree that augments half the symmetric difference with the gap between disjoint subtrees, yielding a geodesic structure under simultaneous growth and shrinkage.
motivation: The symmetric difference metric cannot distinguish whether two disjoint subtrees are close or far apart, so a refined metric is needed to capture spatial separation between subtrees.
method: They halve the symmetric difference, add a term measuring the gap between the subtrees, prove the resulting function is a metric, show a factor-one-half optimality and a canonical embedding of the tree, and interpret the metric as the minimum cost of crawling via growth and shrinkage without jumping.
result: The construction is shown to be a genuine metric with a canonical tree embedding, and with simultaneous growth and shrinkage the space of fixed-length subtrees becomes a geodesic space.
conclusion: The crawling metric provides a geometrically meaningful distance on subtree spaces that resolves the shortcomings of the symmetric difference, enabling geodesic analysis of fixed-size subtrees.

title: Automated Rule Mutation For Emerging Attack Variants Using Infrastructure-Aware Technique Proximity
authors: Sepehr Ghaffarzadegan, Boubakr Nour, Makan Pourzandi, Mourad Debbabi, Chadi Assi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detection rules are typically crafted based on specific observations of an attack. While these rules are effective for particular attack instances, their coverage diminishes when adversaries modify their techniques, such as by employing alternative execution paths or adapting to different telemetry environments while achieving the same objective. To address this challenge, we introduce ARMS, an automated rule mutation solution that generates variant detection rules. ARMS defines a novel three-dimensional proximity space to identify techniques related to the original attack that capture structural relations, functional similarity, and environmental constraints. Rather than relying on ungrounded generation, ARMS leverages verifiable attack execution commands, which are extracted via semantic alignment with the Atomic Red Team repository, to construct a context-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. We evaluated ARMS using verified, public SigmaHQ rules and successfully generated variants, demonstrating ARMS's capability to expand detection coverage. We further evaluated ARMS across multiple research questions, showing the effectiveness of each proximity dimension and infrastructure-aware rule customization. Nearly all generated variant rules successfully compiled into SIEM queries, and ~92% of the newly generated rules detect the original behavior despite attackers' technique variations.
tldr: ARMS automates mutation of cyberattack detection rules by using an infrastructure-aware technique proximity space and a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.
motivation: Static detection rules lose coverage when adversaries modify attack techniques, so vari-ant rules are needed to preserve detection under technique changes.
method: ARMS defines a three-dimensional proximity space over structural, functional, and environmental relations, extracts verifiable Atomic Red Team execution commands, and uses a context-aware RAG pipeline to generate SigmaHQ rule variants.
result: Generated variants compiled into SIEM queries, and about 92% of new rules detected the original behavior despite attacker technique variations.
conclusion: The work improves detection coverage for emerging attack variants, but it is cybersecurity rule engineering and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ration: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control For Ai Agents
authors: Yuntao Du, Harsh Chaudhari, Yuetian Chen, Ron Heichman, Ashish Jayamohan, Kumar Pallav, Mahim Patel, Kaiyuan Zhang, Kyle Polley, Jerry Ma, Ninghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.
tldr: RATION is a risk-based access control framework for AI agents that tracks accumulated measurable risks during task execution to balance security and utility.
motivation: AI agents interacting with external environments face security threats such as indirect prompt injection, while existing action-restriction defenses impose a substantial security-utility trade-off.
method: The framework builds task-specific policies from explicit user constraints and implicit risks calibrated from historical executions, then continuously tracks accumulated risks and applies enforcement strategies by risk type.
result: Experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION maintains strong security and high task utility across diverse models and environments.
conclusion: Quantitative risk-based access control can improve the security-utility trade-off for AI agents compared with purely restrictive action-based defenses.

title: SecODD: Adapting The Operational Design Domain From Driving Autonomy To Autonomous Cyber Defense
authors: Jina Kang, Jeong-Han Yun, Hyesong Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security operations centers are beginning to delegate detection, triage, and containment to Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) agents at execution time. Erroneous high-impact playbooks can disrupt critical services and create accountability gaps among deployers, SOC supervisors, vendors, managed service providers, and infrastructure providers. We propose SecODD, an execution-time governance framework for ACD that adapts the Operational Design Domain concept from autonomous-vehicle regulation to cyber autonomy. It defines the authorized scope of automated defensive actions, models when meaningful human intervention must remain possible, and specifies auditable due-care conditions through a Mitigation Safe Harbor. Four engineering requirements---tamper-evident logging, human-in-the-loop orchestration, rollback playbooks, and safe-state transition controls---are evaluated through a per-scenario audit matrix that illustrates how two ACD failure modes can be translated into pass/fail audit outcomes. The result is an evidence-oriented framework that authorizes ACD only when autonomous actions are bounded, interruptible, recoverable, and reconstructable from evidence.
tldr: SecODD adapts the Operational Design Domain concept from autonomous-vehicle regulation to govern autonomous cyber defense agents at execution time.
motivation: Security operations centers are delegating detection, triage, and containment to autonomous agents, where erroneous high-impact playbooks can disrupt services and create accountability gaps among deployers, vendors, and providers.
method: The authors define an execution-time governance framework specifying authorized scope of automated defensive actions, conditions for meaningful human intervention, and auditable due-care via a Mitigation Safe Harbor, evaluated through four engineering requirements (tamper-evident logging, human-in-the-loop orchestration, rollback playbooks, safe-state transitions) in a per-scenario audit matrix.
result: Two illustrative ACD failure modes are translated into pass/fail audit outcomes, yielding an evidence-oriented framework that authorizes autonomy only when actions are bounded, interruptible, recoverable, and reconstructable.
conclusion: The work offers a policy-and-engineering governance template for cyber autonomy, but has no connection to quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Locate, Then Reason: End-to-End Patch Presence Testing In Stripped Binaries
authors: Huaijin Wang, Tongda Wang, Zhibo Liu, Yue Zhang, Shuai Wang, Pengfei Hu, Jianzhong Liu, Fangtian Zhong, Shaohua Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.25071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary patch presence testing (PPT) determines whether a security fix is present in a stripped binary. Prior systems often assume that patch-relevant code is known or successfully matched. Function-level matching is brittle to compilation changes, inlining, finite model context, and missing usage context; moreover, similarity suppresses the patch-sized distinction needed for the verdict. We present PatchAlign, an end-to-end binary PPT workflow, which performs large-scale localization that maximizes recall economically, then the final verdict reasons for patch-specific evidence. PatchAlign uses instruction-aligned retrieval and caller-callee context to accurately locate patch-relevant binary code pieces, then screens the shortlist and compares target binary code with vulnerable and patched references using an LLM. Our experiments indicate that PatchAlign can precisely localize patch-relevant code and determine patch status without a target-location oracle.
tldr: PatchAlign is an end-to-end workflow that detects whether a security patch is present in stripped binaries by localizing patch-relevant code with instruction-aligned retrieval and then reasoning over vulnerable/patched references using an LLM.
motivation: Prior binary patch presence testing systems assume patch-relevant code is known or can be matched at function granularity, which is brittle to compilation changes, inlining, limited model context, and missing usage context, while similarity metrics blur the patch-sized distinctions needed for a verdict.
method: The approach performs large-scale, recall-oriented localization using instruction-aligned retrieval plus caller-callee context to identify candidate patch-relevant code pieces, then screens the shortlist and compares the target code against vulnerable and patched references via an LLM to reason about patch-specific evidence.
result: Experiments show PatchAlign can precisely localize patch-relevant code and correctly determine patch status without relying on a target-location oracle.
conclusion: Decoupling localization from verdict reasoning and grounding the final decision in patch-specific evidence enables accurate, oracle-free binary patch presence testing in stripped binaries.

title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization With Fully First-Order Oracles
authors: Shanshui Niu Qihao Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.24538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point [MATH] satisfying [MATH] within [MATH] component-gradient calls, where [MATH] is the total number of components and [MATH] is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length [MATH] with batches of size [MATH]. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on [MATH] and [MATH] is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed [MATH].
